speechtext:

Whereas the Canadian taxpayer is taking a beating through the action of the Canadian government in buying foreign oil at double the price of oil which could be purchased from Alberta which if bought here would, in addition, keep the money and the jobs in Canada, therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Calgary South (Mr. Thomson):
That the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources start negotiating for a change with the government of Alberta or, alternatively, accept the offer made by Premier Lougheed last year which would bring benefits to all Canadians.

subsubtopic: PLAN TO CURB JAPANESE CAR IMPORTS-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, as we all know, there are serious problems within the North American auto industry operating here in Canada. The solution to these problems has been compounded by the degree to which export vehicles are entering Canada, particularly from Japan. At the moment the United States and Japan are in the final stages of an agreement to limit Japanese auto imports to the United States. Most experts are of the opinion that this could and will cause severe problems in Canada. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles):
That the government, being aware of the likelihood of economic damage caused by Japanese autos being dumped in our market, be required to produce within thirty days its plan to deal with this urgent matter, and further, that the government consider the initiatives being taken by other countries in defence of their own workers.

speechtext:

That this House condemns the Grit cabinet for its numerous gross violations of the mobility rights of Canadians and, in particular, its failure to allow any secretary, living anywhere in Canada, the opportunity to compete for a job in one of our diplomatic missions, to serve Canada in other countries.

subsubtopic: CALL FOR NEW POLICY-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43. Whereas the national energy policy is in complete chaos and has proven a national disaster; and whereas it is essential a policy be devised which will provide Canadians with a secure supply of energy and the rapid development of Canadian oil and gas to provide jobs and incomes for Canadians across this land, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Towers):
First, that the government move immediately to rescind its national energy policy. Second, that an all-party special committee of Parliament be formed with power to hold hearings in the maritimes, in central and northern Canada and in the west, with the oil industry and other interested and involved Canadians, in order to establish a rational and reasonable national energy policy which will work.

subsubtopic: TELEX MESSAGE FROM PREMIER LYON OF MANITOBA-QUERY RESPECTING RESPONSE BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is to the Prime Minister, who on Friday received a telex from Premier Lyon, the chairman of the provincial premiers conference, indicating that eight of the provinces have negotiated and come to an agreement on what Premier Lyon describes as a new Canadian patriation plan, including an amending formula. The premier went on to ask that the Prime Minister suspend parliamentary consideration of the resolution and agree to join the provincial premiers at the conference table to achieve the goal of a made-in-Canada Constitution.

April 6, 1981
Oral Questions
My question to the Prime Minister is whether he will respond positively to that very positive initiative taken by eight provinces, adjourn the debate on the matter in the House of Commons, and meet the premiers to discuss a made-in-Canada Constitution.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: TELEX MESSAGE FROM PREMIER LYON OF MANITOBA-QUERY RESPECTING RESPONSE BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the short answer is no. The longer answer is that I still continue to entertain very grave doubts about the veracity of the statement that they have reached agreement. We have been told that many times before. The agreement has never been forthcoming.
In this particular case we know from Mr. Ryan that he would not attend such a meeting. I presume he has not been consulted on the formula. Mr. Ryan is the leader of the party which, just last week, the Leader of the Opposition was saying would presumably win the election.
We know from Mr. Levesque that he has seen some vague draft, but I am convinced that if he had seen anything which is near to an agreement he would be making it public, as would be his duty during a provincial election campaign, so that the people would know if it is good for them and the people of Canada, or if it is just another bluff on the part of the premiers.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR ADJOURNMENT OF DEBATE ON CONSTITUTIONAL RESOLUTION

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: REQUEST FOR ADJOURNMENT OF DEBATE ON CONSTITUTIONAL RESOLUTION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I must express not only regret at the Prime Minister's response but at the tone of that response, in which he calls into question the veracity of the eight provincial premiers of the country who have worked through the summer, worked through the winter, and sent a telex to him. I think that indicates Canada has reached a new low in federal-provincial relations caused by the unreasonable position taken by the Prime Minister of Canada.
The question I have for the Prime Minister is this. Will he at least consider delaying and adjourning debate in this House on the constitutional resolution until the people of Quebec have the opportunity to elect a government on April 13, and then be prepared to discuss with the seven other premiers and whatever party forms the government of the province of Quebec the possibility of meeting, so that we can discuss and resolve here in Canada this Canadian question in a Canadian way of agreement, rather than aggravating and deepening the differences in Canada by the Prime Minister pursuing his own path and standing up in the House of Commons to insult the integrity of eight provincial premiers?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: REQUEST FOR ADJOURNMENT OF DEBATE ON CONSTITUTIONAL RESOLUTION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, once again we have the key strategy of the Tory party in this question. Once again the Leader of the Opposition wants delay. First it was delay because of the substance, then it was delay because of the process, then it was delay because of the courts, and now it is delay because of the premiers. It has been quite clear that that is the only capacity
of the Tory party for decision. It is not to make up its mind, it is to seek delay.
If anything characterizes this Parliament and this House of Commons, it is that it must take its responsibility for its actions. When a former leader of that party used to call this the supreme court-Parliament-he was following a valid doctrine in political theory and in parliamentary terms, Certainly he would not have suggested that this House not take its responsibility when faced with a serious question like that and wait for the premiers or for the courts to give us their blessing.

subtopic: POSITION TAKEN BY PRIME MINISTER ON TIMING OF FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL MEETINGS

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: POSITION TAKEN BY PRIME MINISTER ON TIMING OF FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL MEETINGS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the purpose of this party, and I would hope of this Parliament, is to keep this country Canada together and not to drive it apart through unilateral, stubborn action on the part of the Prime Minister.
May I ask the Prime Minister whether it is his position that the Government of Canada will under no circumstances meet with provincial premiers to discuss a Canadian way to bring our Constitution home and to amend it here, until his personal resolution has been rammed through the House of Commons by whatever means?

subtopic: POSITION TAKEN BY PRIME MINISTER ON TIMING OF FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL MEETINGS
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subtopic: POSITION TAKEN BY PRIME MINISTER ON TIMING OF FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL MEETINGS
speechtext: Is that the position of the Government of Canada, that there will be no discussion until he has had his way with his resolution?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: POSITION TAKEN BY PRIME MINISTER ON TIMING OF FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL MEETINGS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the expression "rammed through the House" seems a little bit hyperbolic when one realizes we have been debating this very subject for six months; that is hardly a ramming procedure. It has given six months to the premiers in order to come up with a resolution or some kind of a suggestion. Now they are telling us to wait again, and the Tory leader is supporting them.
The question was: would I meet with the premiers? I have pointed out that the resolution before the House provides for two years of meetings to find an amending formula which would be the result of a consensus between the premiers and the Government of Canada; two years to do that. If the premiers have indeed made some progress, which I continue to think unlikely or implausible, they could tell us now. We could, within days of having our own Constitution in Canada, convene that meeting. We could use the formula provided in the resolution to have whatever amending formula we could all agree upon. Failing agreement, we could have the people decide on the differences of opinion between some premiers and the federal government and some other premiers. So the meeting, if indeed it is fruitful, will not be lost, because we will meet with them as soon as we have our Constitution, and get
April 6, 1981

this magic amending formula which they say will be good for Canada.

subtopic: POSITION TAKEN BY PRIME MINISTER ON TIMING OF FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL MEETINGS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: POSITION TAKEN BY PRIME MINISTER ON TIMING OF FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL MEETINGS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, let me be clear about this question which goes to the heart of our ability to exist and to prevail as a nation. Has the Prime Minister of Canada ruled out absolutely the possibility of any meeting with the premiers of the country to discuss a patriation package and an amending formula before his own personal resolution is passed by the House of Commons?

PROCEDURE RELATING TO CONDUCT OF FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Right Hon. Prime Minister. No matter what are the differences in the House or in the country, I think there is a certain manner in which all of us expect federal-provincial relations to be conducted; not by raising the veracity of the other partners in confederation, nor having them described as a cabal or a gang of eight by one of the members of the government back row.
In view of the fact that the Prime Minister has now rejected meeting with the premiers, despite the formal request by the chairman of the premiers, has the Prime Minister replied formally to the premiers that he will not meet with them? Has he given them the reasons why he will not meet with them, or are federal-provincial relations now to be conducted by press comment, media assessment or, for that matter, by comments made from abroad?

subtopic: PROCEDURE RELATING TO CONDUCT OF FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the opposition seems to make much of the statement that I doubted the veracity of the premiers in saying they had reached agreement. speechtext:
Madam Speaker, we are dealing with a purely hypothetical situation. I suspect that some of the premiers have no interest in making the formula-if they have one-public at this time because of upcoming elections. 1 do not want to deal with a hypothetical question. I dealt with ministers three months on this question, and I have no reason to believe now that there will be agreement among the eight

premiers. They could not agree in the summer. We explored all avenues. The checkerboard proposition they made was not even accepted by the hon. member in the committee because he proposed another type of amending formula which was completely different from the Vancouver formula. I am quite sure there will be no such thing.
What disappoints me most in the statement of Premier Lyon is that he did not refer at all to the charter of rights. subsubtopic: APPLICATION TO FEDERAL CIVIL SERVANTS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is to the President of the Treasury Board. In some ways it follows the statement of the Minister of Justice about a charter of rights for all Canadians.
Earlier today the Canadian Labour Congress in a paper entitled "A Strategy for Workplace Health and Safety in the 1980s" called for changes to Part IV of the Canada Labour Code. On page 7 of that report it says:
The proposed new legislation must apply equally and without any reservations to all workplaces and undertakings in the federal jurisdiction. Activities such as uranium mining and processing, the entire transportation sector, or the federal civil service are examples of undertakings which must be included without exception under the coverage of the new law.
With that and the recent statement of the Minister of Justice in mind, is the President of the Treasury Board willing to guarantee that federal civil servants will come under any new legislation under Part IV of the Canada Labour Code?

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald J. Johnston (President of the Treasury Board):
subsubtopic: APPLICATION TO FEDERAL CIVIL SERVANTS
speechtext: No, Madam Speaker, I would not give such a guarantee, but I would guarantee that the protection enjoyed by federal civil servants will be at least equal to, if not exceed, that provided by Part IV of the Canada Labour Code.

Madam Speaker, the problem is that the present system does not provide protection. Protective clothing is not required for meat inspectors in Agriculture Canada. There are three lab technicians who have liver damage. They are being told to be careful. There is the infamous example of Les Terrasses de la Chaudiere, where asbestos and formaldehyde have been found in the atmosphere but, because of overlap and lack of guidelines, the workers there are calling it "Les Terrasses of Shoddy Air." That is what is happening. We cannot trust directives.

subsubtopic: PROVISION OF SERVICE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, that is certainly not an accurate characterization of the direction I gave to the RCMP last week. If it was reported in that way, then I am glad to have this opportunity to set the matter straight.
The Government of Canada is anxious to continue providing RCMP services to those provinces which have been using them in the past. We have been negotiating for seven months to try to reach new agreements to take effect as of last Tuesday. The negotiations have gone slower than I would have liked. Thus, the contracts expired without a new agreement.
I indicated to the provinces that we would be prepared to continue providing the services without a new cost-sharing agreement, while we try to reach a new cost-sharing agreement. British Columbia understood this and there has been an exchange of letters which has led the RCMP services to continue there while bona fide negotiations are being carried on. But when I went to work on Friday morning I received a bombshell from the Attorney General of Saskatchewan. Mr. Romanow indicated that he will only accept continued RCMP services on the basis of the cost-sharing agreement which expired. For seven months I have been saying that those terms would not be renewed, that we wanted new terms and we were willing to negotiate them.
April 6, 1981

We are willing to provide the services without an agreement, but we are not willing to continue providing services on a price unilaterally imposed by the provinces.
Some four or five other provinces have joined with Saskatchewan in insisting that services will only be accepted on the basis of the old price. At law, if you continue to provide services when the other party imposes a price, you are stuck with that price. That is not acceptable to Canada. In the next few hours I am hoping to talk to the attorneys general.
When I phoned Mr. Romanow on Friday his executive assistant told me that Mr. Romanow's schedule did not permit him to come to the telephone to speak to me about his telegram. I hope that I will meet with him in the next little while.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is for the Solicitor General. The Solicitor General, supported not surprisingly by Quebec Liberal leader Claude Ryan, has refused to implement the legislation of the province of Quebec extending the right to vote to prisoners in federal institutions in the upcoming Quebec election.
I have before me a copy of the confidential minutes of the February ministerial conference on human rights at which the Solicitor General promised:
But for those provinces that decide to extend the right to vote in their elections to inmates over whom we have custody-I wanted to indicate that we are prepared to do everything we can to see that your law is given effect in the institutions-
Why is the Solicitor General now changing his mind and reneging on this commitment made to the province of Quebec and denying some 2,000 prisoners their fundamental democratic right to vote, as passed by the legislature of Quebec?

subsubtopic: EXERCISE OF FRANCHISE BY PENITENTIARY INMATES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I stand by what I said, as quoted by the hon. member. But I am not satisfied that the system which was put forward by the province of Quebec will work within the institutions in the province of Quebec. I have indicated that I will watch with interest during the provincial election to see whether fair elections can be held with due respect to order and security without violating the privacy of particular inmates. I am not certain that it can be done. If it can be done, then I stand by my undertaking that we would be prepared in the future to accommodate any provincial legislation within federal institutions.
I indicated at the same time that the Parliament of Canada has not extended the right to vote to prisoners. That is a matter for each legislature or for Parliament to decide within the limits of its own franchise. The strong view was expressed by all but a very few of the attorneys general who were present, that inmates did not deserve the right to vote while they were incarcerated, and I agree with that.

My supplementary question relates to another group of inmates who were denied voting rights, namely, those who were held on remand in provincial institutions during federal elections. The Solicitor General also knows these inmates are presumed to be innocent. subsubtopic: TELIDON
speechtext:
In so far as the
Department of Communications is concerned, the answer to the above question is as follows: 1. The Department of Communications did not exhibit Telidon at INTELCOM 80 because of funding and human resource limitations which restricted the department's attendance to a limited number of important trade expositions and conferences. However, much has been accomplished within the previous promotional budget. For example, there have been approximately 75 distinct promotional activities since June, 1980, including attendance at several international expositions and conferences. In addition, there have been publicity tours in the U.S.A. and West Germany and one recently completed in Australia. The department's Telidon program strategy, in conjunction with the Departments of Industry, Trade and Commerce and External Affairs, is to assist Canadian industry wherever possible within approved budgets to acquire contracts for field trials and operational Telidon systems in the U.S.A., Europe, Latin America and Australia.
2. The department was indeed aware that the French Antiope system would be exhibited. The French government is supporting Antiope with a large promotion budget which permits the exhibition of Antiope in virtually all important trade shows and conferences.
3.	It is difficult to obtain authenticated figures for the exact promotional budgets of the competing British (Prestel) and French (Antiope) systems. However, both countries have specific marketing branches in the U.S.A. called Aregon and Sofratev respectively. The science counsellor of the Canadian embassy in Washington, D.C. has estimated that the British are spending approximately $10 million to $15 million per year for the promotional activities in the U.S.A. alone and the French some $20 million per year. The respected British Organization Communications Systems and Planning Ltd. has stated that British government expenditures to date are in excess of $84 million and annual expenditures are currently running at $42 million. Equal or greater investments are being made by the British industry.
4.	At the time of the INTELCOM 80 exhibition, the department's total Telidon budget from FY 79/80 to the end of the Telidon program in FY 82/83 was $13,241 million. Since recent cabinet approval of the augmented Telidon funding, this figure will rise to $40,341 million. This amount and the portion allotted for promotion (including standards and industrial strategy) is broken down by fiscal year as follows:

5.	Within the research sector's Telidon program the promotional activities are primarily carried out by the directorate of applications development containing three permanent staff and four term employees. Its functions are to develop and implement promotional activities, to contribute to international standardization activities, to work with other groups for the development and implementation of industrial and marketing strategies, to facilitate technology transfer to industry and to identify new research and development work. Other sectors within the department contribute much to promotion as well. The international telecommunications branch of the policy sector has provided assistance in both international marketing and legal matters. The information services section of the deputy minister's office gives continuous aid in the execution of promotional exhibits. Outside the department, of course, External Affairs and Industry, Trade and Commerce provide continuing assistance. Recently a marketing-promotion committee has been established with representation from all three departments.
6.	The government has not considered transferring primary responsibility for promoting Telidon to other departments although considerable assistance is being given by the Departments of Industry, Trade and Commerce and External Affairs. The reasons relate to both experience and budget. First, the
April 6, 1981

department considers its group of technical experts which invented and developed Telidon in the first place essential for the promotion of what is still a fledgling technology which though recognized as the world's superior videotex and teletext technology is still threatened by the financially massive marketing efforts of its competitors. Secondly, other departments do not have promotional budgets substantially greater than those of the Telidon program. 2.	What were the effects of the ionosphere in Canada's auroral zone and the radar properties of the sea surface on the performance of the synthetic aperture radar being tested in the experiment?

speakeroldname: Mrs. Ursula Appolloni (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
subsubtopic: SEASAT U.S.-SURVEILLANCE SATELLITE
speechtext:
1. Yes.
2.	Auroral activity did not produce detectable effects on the performance of the SEASAT synthetic aperture radar (SAR). However, experiments indicated that the SAR images would be degraded during severe magnetic storms. The radar was optimized to image ocean waves and validation experiments showed the wavelengths between 100 and 500 metres and significant wave heights between 1 and 3.5 metres could be measured. Ships 100 metres long could be detected when moving slowly on a calm sea but even large ships were concealed by the sea clutter from waves during the storm. Often a ship moving at high speed could be detected only by its wake. The radar proved capable of producing usable imagery through rain and snow.
3.	The U.S. SEASAT A experiment and the Canadian surveillance satellite (SURSAT) program have demonstrated the technical feasibility of a spaceborne synthetic aperture radar system for environmental surveillance, particularly of

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1981-82 SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it gives me a great deal of pleasure to address this body today on the borrowing authority bill. I would particularly like to address myself to the imposition of closure. A rose by any other name is still a rose and closure is still closure, which we know is taking place on this measure.

April 6, 1981
Borrowing Authority Act, 1981-82
I would like to draw the attention of the House to the fact that, while this House is considering a bill authorizing the borrowing of $14 billion to run government business, there exists a situation in northeastern Alberta which I can only describe as deplorable. The Bigstone band, in company with their chief, William Beaver, are on a trek from Wabasca in northeastern Alberta to Edmonton to draw attention to their plight. They are asking for financial assistance for their community so that poverty can be alleviated as well as unemployment, which reaches beyond 75 per cent.
I draw this set of circumstances to your attention, Mr. Speaker, because we have a government which has exercised no restraint whatsoever with respect to the economy. It is prepared to borrow $14 billion just to keep operating. A very small fraction of that sum of money could be used in a permanent way to aid in the alleviation of the conditions in many Indian communities, but, more particularly, the Big-stone band in Wabasca. The chief and council, indeed the people of the Bigstone band, decided on this action to draw attention to their plight after a 14-year-old girl, who looked around the community on her birthday and felt that life was no longer worth living, committed suicide. She committed suicide because of the lack of funding, lack of opportunity, lack of jobs and abject poverty that all people in the Wabasca reserve face. I find it difficult to comprehend a government which has set priorities in the way that this government has. It is borrowing $14 billion to run a government when a very small portion of that sum could begin to alleviate the suffering, inequality and lack of jobs which exist on the Bigstone Reserve.
Consider the mortality rates on the Indian reserves in comparison with the national deaths per thousand figures for each age group during the period 1973-76. In the age group one to four years, we find the mortality rate of Indian populations on reserves to be 3.1 deaths per thousand as compared to the national average of 0.8 deaths per thousand. This is over three times the national average. In the age group five to 19 years, the rate is 1.9 per thousand as compared with the national average of 0.7 deaths per thousand. Some of these deaths on Indian reserves are the result of suicide. The figures are very alarming when one looks at the age group 20 to 44 years. The mortality rate for the non,-Indian population in this age group is 1.5 per thousand, while the rate for the Indian population is six per thousand. I would like to point out that this is the age group in which men and women marry and have families.
Can you imagine, Mr. Speaker, the total worthlessness a man must feel, day after day, going home to face his family and children knowing that he cannot provide for them? Can you imagine how devastating this can be to a man's or woman's ego? I find it deplorable that we are forcing our native people into this position. The government should take a minute portion of that $14 billion and aim it at alleviating poverty and creating jobs in native communities, a situation where men and women can hold up their heads and where Indian parents are able to provide for their families as every
member of this House can and, indeed, as every Canadian across our nation wants to do. There is absolutely no future for young Indian people growing up on a reserve.
I would like to outline the events of the last six months. Chief William Beaver, a very honourable man who wants to create a situation on his reserve where men can be employed and the children have an equal opportunity to that experienced elsewhere in Canada, says that he wants to reduce welfare and create jobs. The budget on the reserve was cut to a point where they had to lay off 17 workers at the sawmill. This was a project they had initiated themselves. Seventeen men had to be laid off and were forced to go on welfare. More importantly, logs were left in the bush. In northern Alberta you cannot leave logs in the bush over the winter because they rot in the muskeg. Their whole work for the winter is down the tube because there is no way those logs will survive until the summer; they will be rotted.
The doors of the band office had to be closed because there was no money to pay the workers who were all laid off. There is now one girl at the Bigstone band office who is answering the phone. All the economic programs they had designed and were working on to create employment and give a sense of pride to the Indian people of the Bigstone band have been stopped. The Bigstone band members are forced to walk 400 kilometres from their band office in northeastern Alberta to Edmonton to draw attention to their plight. For the past ten days they have been attempting to negotiate with the minister of manpower because he is responsible for such negotiations. He has been appointed as negotiator with the band but he has failed to meet with them.
On Friday the minister indicated that he was prepared to speak and negotiate with the Bigstone band. One half hour after that statement in the House of Commons, the chief got a telephone call from the regional office in Edmonton informing him that the minister was grounded in Ottawa and could not leave. Therefore, he could not sit down with them and negotiate.
I ask, where are the priorities here? The government is prepared to spend $60 million on an advertising campaign, yet a very small percentage of that amount can save lives. This march from the Wabasca area by the Bigstone band was precipitated by the death of a young girl, 14 years old, who decided on her birthday that she did not see it worth while to live in that community under conditions of abject poverty and with no future.
Not one cabinet minister from this government has said that he would be prepared to sit down with the Bigstone band chief and his council. It is a deplorable situation in Canada when elderly people, young people-I am talking particularly about them-people with arthritis, have marched 400 kilometres to bring attention to their plight. However, the very sad thing is that although they are getting some attention from the media, the attention of the government is not being focused on the problem. The government is ignoring them completely. It is
April 6, 1981

warning them: "Do not occupy offices, do not do that sort of thing, or we will not be able to deal with you". I find that to be a very sad situation indeed.
If one looks at the social support expenditures of all federal programs for native people, one finds that they are increasing dramatically in some areas. But support for economic development programs is decreasing dramatically. The Indian people in Canada do not want handouts. They do not want to be on welfare. They do not want to go home at night to face their children, knowing every day that they cannot provide for those children in the same manner as you and I, Mr. Speaker, can provide for our children. Can one imagine the very devastating effect this must have on these people who face their families every day knowing they do not have proper nourishment and that they cannot supply the basic needs of their children because they are on welfare? They want jobs. They are marching for economic equality.
Mr. Speaker, $14 billion, if we say it fast enough, looks pretty good. It is very difficult to equate what $14 billion means and what it will buy. The Wabasca band, the Bigstone band, is asking less than 1 per cent of that amount of money- 0.2 per cent. This would launch an economic development program on this reserve which is completely surrounded by the tar sands and oil companies doing exploration work. They want to be trained so they can take jobs which are now available around their area. They sit on the bridge in the summertime and watch the trucks go by day after day, through the reserve, to the in situ plants, the experimental plants which are working in the area.
They see neighbouring their reserve ranchers who are raising cattle and producing feed for their cattle, and yet they are systematically dropping further and further behind because they do not have the necessary expertise. They need training, and money is needed to provide this training. Some of the men I talked to are still surviving on trap lines and have not used welfare. However, they are now finding that their trap lines are being destroyed by the encroachment of civilization on to the reserve. There is no compensation for that. You cannot compensate a man for the loss of his business and life's work with a settlement of $10,000.
The government is doing absolutely nothing for these people. The Department of Indian Affairs is responsible for them under the treaties. In fact, all governments at the federal level have that distinct responsibility to the native people, who were the first citizens of Canada.
We must examine economic conditions surrounding reserves in Canada. I particularly ask that the government sit down and negotiate with the Bigstone band at Wabasca, the chief, and his council, so that they can do a survey on economic conditions, prepare a minerals inventory, examine job opportunities and draw up a general plan so that the people of the Bigstone band can participate in the economic development which is taking place around them.
Can anyone imagine a 14-year-old girl taking her life on her birthday because she sees absolutely no future for herself? We must address ourselves to this problem. We must develop the
Borrowing Authority Act, 1981-82
reserves in exactly the same way as we are prepared to support the Department of Regional Economic Expansion to help the have-not areas of the provinces.
On Saturday of last week I met with the chief and council of the Bigstone band. They were amazed that Canadians would allow some of their elderly people to walk 400 kilometers. One arthritic lady, 65 years old, walked with her grandchildren. They were amazed that there is a need in Canada to do this kind of thing before anyone will pay attention to their plight. I say that is a shame on every one of us in this House. We must do something to assist the Bigstone band gain economic equality in northeastern Alberta.
The borrowing authority bill will be passed, Mr. Speaker; and the money will be spent on a number of frivolous programs, such as the advertising program to sell the centralist view on the Constitution and on the energy program to the rest of Canada. It will be used to sell a number of ideas that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) might have. I ask that we, as the representatives of our areas, as legislators, urge the government and the cabinet to consult with the Bigstone band. I ask that the government take just a small portion of the funds being borrowed and redirect them to the Bigstone band. This would allow the band to continue its economic development so that its people can take their place in society, walk straight, be proud of their heritage and so their children can see a future for themselves.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1981-82 SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to begin by congratulating the hon. member for Athabasca (Mr. Shields) for reminding all of us in this House of the importance of the fact that there are in Canada today, and not only in his constituency, millions of Canadians living in conditions of poverty, ignored by their government and by their fellow citizens.
Since we are discussing today the fact that the government is asking for authority to borrow some $14 billion, it is very important to remember the purposes for which the money is intended and the people who are affected by the programs that have been established. In the last six months that we have been debating the Constitution, we have heard a great deal about the alienation of groups of Canadians from their government and particularly western alienation; in fact, we have heard a great deal from the hon. member for Athabasca about western alienation.
I should like to suggest that there is a deeper kind of alienation in all of Canada, and that is the very real problem that most Canadians do not have a voice in Parliament. When they see what we do here, they cannot recognize this House as a forum in which their views and concerns are being expressed. The government is so preoccupied with one question, that is, the formal arrangements under which we govern ourselves- and that is all a constitution is, the formalities of constitutional life-that it has forgotten about the fundamentals of a society. The questions are, how does a society feed itself and what do people pay for food? How does a society clothe itself and what

April 6, 1981
Borrowing Authority Act, 1981-82
do people pay for clothing? How does a society house itself and what do people pay for housing? Do people have jobs or not? Do we have an economic policy? When people hear us talk about monetarism and all the other subjects we talk about, they feel very remote from us. The real question is, do we have a government which is as concerned about and determined to deal with the economy and the human problems that face the average Canadian as it is with all the other matters that so obviously preoccupy it?
I say to my western friends in the House, as I have said in my own caucus, that of course there is western alienation, and for very good reason. There is a variety of reasons which go back into our history. Central Canadian financial institutions have played a dominant role and a national policy has been created which has meant that the hinterlands in the east and the west of the country were used as metropolitan centres; and, of course, that has created resentment.
I suggest there is a deeper kind of alienation at work in the country today. It applies not only to people living in Alberta or in the constituency of Athabasca, about whom the hon. member spoke so eloquently this afternoon, but even to those in my riding, which is in the very shadow of Bay Street. From my home I can look across the Don Valley and see the towers lit up at night, yet the people in my constituency are just as alienated from the large economic forces that control them and from their government. When they look to their government or to their Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), do they see a government or a Prime Minister who knows the cost of a loaf of bread? Do they see a government or a Prime Minister who responds to inflation, which is 20 per cent higher than predicted in the budget of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Mac-Eachen)? Do they see a government that is prepared to act with a degree of fairness when it comes to treating the most powerful economic figures and the most vulnerable people on the same terms? Do they see a government or a Prime Minister that can respond to the broader, abstract, structural problems in our economy about which I and many members of my caucus have spoken on the few occasions when we have had the opportunity to speak on the economy in the last few months? Do we have a government which understands what it means to be unemployed, to be living in poverty, to have 60 per cent of our senior citizens living below the poverty line?
Many hon. members speak about Ontario as if it were some vast, wealthy, opulent province-as if no one in Ontario is poor, or knows what it means to be out of work. I have taken the opportunity to travel to and speak in every province, Mr. Speaker. I have talked to people all across the country. I would invite people to look behind the billboards and the so-called image of affluence which is projected from central Canada and see some of the hard realities that face every Canadian, whether they live in Ontario, Quebec, the maritimes, Newfoundland or the west.
The reality is that we have a government which does not understand the basic social and economic problems which face the average Canadian. That was the problem with the Crosbie budget. It was the budget which dealt with abstractions and
not with the problems which face the average Canadian. That is the problem with the MacEachen budget and it is the problem that we face now with the government saying, "Give us another $14 billion so we can borrow and get our house in order."
I should like to deal briefly with some of the basic problems that face the country. The request in this borrowing authority bill for $14 billion is a strange one. As consumers, we frequently face the prospect of going into a bank, a credit union or a trust company to ask whether we can borrow a lot of money, or even a small amount of money. The first question which the bank manager will ask is, "What are you doing with the money you are borrowing?" I have always compared the granting of borrowing authority with that basic question. Of course, the sums are much larger. The amount of $14 billion is almost inconceivable to the average person. It is about 20 per cent of what the government spends in a year. It is a very substantial sum of money.
Let me come back to the basic question, "What are you using this money for?" Instead of borrowing money to invest or to ensure that eventually we will be out of debt, this government's budgetary policy is to borrow money to pay for groceries.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1981-82 SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY
speechtext: Yesterday's groceries.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1981-82 SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY
speechtext:
That is the critical problem facing the government.
There are two kinds of debt. There is the budgetary deficit, money that we borrow, money which the government is asking for now, in order to pay for its own expenditures. Then because of increased imports, our balance of payments with the rest of the world is in a deficit position. That is the second kind of debt that we have.
One would have thought that the intelligent way to run the budget of Canada would be to say, "We have these two kinds of debt, and in order to get out of debt we will borrow money and invest it." That would seem to me the basic thrust of the position, taking for granted, as we do in this party, that there are occasions when it is perfectly appropriate for the government to borrow money and go into debt.
I would remind hon. members that there are times when it is perfectly appropriate for the average citizen to go into debt. For example, it is perfectly appropriate for the average citizen to go into debt to buy a house. I do not know anyone in my party who is in a position to buy a house outright. For example, I do not know anyone in my party who could go to Vancouver, where the average price of a house is $171,000, and pay for it in cash. I see the hon. member for Edmonton North (Mr. Paproski) is smiling. Maybe he is in a position to do that.

I have the same problem as any member of this Elouse who is not wealthy. I am wealthy in one way, and that is because I have a wonderful wife and family and I can look after their needs.

speechtext: Oh, oh!

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1981-82 SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY
speechtext:
Might I say to the hon. member that my reference was made only in fun.
There are economic decisions which we as individuals make requiring us to go into debt. When we go to the bank, the credit union or the trust company and ask to borrow, say, $5,000 for a $55,000 mortgage on a house, the lending institution will want to look at the reasonableness of the investment being made and of the request to borrow. A mortgage is probably the biggest debt most of us will ever take on, but we are taking on this debt because we want to own something and think that our investment and our equity share in it will grow.
Let us look at what the government is doing in the energy sector. The government's general economic policy does not make any kind of sense. What this government has said, and what the Conservative Party said when it was in government, is that the question of who owns our economy is not an important one. I say the real problem facing our country is that we are in a position of being, as it were, tenants in our own land. We are industrial tenants. Look at how little research and development takes place in Canada, Mr. Speaker. In the automobile industry, for example, we find we are simply tenants. We are trying to get a better deal for our automobile workers, but they work in an industry that is entirely foreign controlled. We are trying to get a better deal for people in other industries, also entirely foreign controlled. But let us not be under any illusions that we are really in an ownership position in those industries.
In the oil and gas industry, Imperial Oil is 70 per cent controlled by Exxon. That company will be totally unaffected by the government's energy policy. In fact, Imperial Oil will probably grow, for a reason which I will come to in a moment. Shell Oil is 70 per cent controlled by the international company. If we go right down the list, we can see that all of the largest actors in the oil and gas sector, with one exception, Petro-Canada, are owned and controlled by outside economic interests and we have become tenants.
Borrowing Authority Act, 1981-82
The oil and gas sector will grow in value and importance. This sector will be vitally important over the next five or ten years. The price of the resource will increase because of scarcity. All parties agree the price must go up. The only question is how far and how fast, and who will get the revenue. Everyone is agreed that prices are going to rise.
There are various ways, which I can detail, to take over ownership of that industry as Canadians, as provinces, as the federal government, as credit unions, as co-operative institutions and as small businesses. Everyone in a mixed economy will move in this area. The government could have come to us and said it wants to borrow so it can invest in human capital and resources, that it has decided we can no longer survive economically by automatically condemning 10 per cent or 15 per cent of our young people coming out of secondary schools across Canada to unemployment. In some parts of my constituency, the unemployment rate among young people 16 and 17 years old is upwards of 35 per cent and 40 per cent.
This is not the problem the government is going to tackle. It is not going to invest capital in order to reduce and solve basic economic problems, either in the field of human resources or energy. The government has no strategy, plan or organized intention to deal with fundamental problems. It says, along with many members of the Conservative Party, that we cannot afford greater Canadian ownership at the present time, that we cannot afford to take on the multinationals in the oil and gas industry. That is the position of the Conservative Party: we cannot afford it because it will be detrimental to self-sufficiency. Just this past weekend there was a takeover of MacMillan Bloedel by Noranda. I did not hear any member of the Conservative party saying Noranda could not afford to do that. I did not hear them say that takeovers and acquisitions like that are a waste of money.
There is a very simple reason why it is not a waste of money. In fact, the whole logic of the capitalist system is that takeovers and mergers mean a greater concentration in the system. That is one of the problems or diseases of the system. The reason is that you are acquiring an asset of which the value can only increase. Noranda made a decision to acquire the assets of MacMillan Bloedel. Those assets will grow with inflation, and their value will accrue to them.
Two hundred years ago a movement was born in western Europe. It started with the trade unions and co-ops and in the last century grew to a political movement which has spread throughout the world. And it is a movement that says, "If the logic of capitalism is corporate acquisition and there is no longer any competition, and if the only effect of these acquisitions is that a few absentee landlords and absentee shareholders receive the benefit of these assets without having laboured other than staying home and opening the envelopes which had the coupons in them, then why shouldn't the assets, and the dividends that flow from the assets, accrue to the people?"

April 6, 1981
Borrowing Authority Act, 1981-82

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1981-82 SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY
speechtext: How many dividends has Petro-Canada paid?

speechtext:
The hon. member asks how many dividends Petro-Can has paid. My answer is "not enough". In the province of Saskatchewan this year, the potash corporation paid a dividend to the people of Saskatchewan.
There is no reason that we should be suffering under a government with no over-all economic strategy and no general purpose and understanding of the structural problems of the economy. The government says it is in favour of Canadianiza-tion. If you look ahead ten years at the oil and gas sector, its policies will leave us with less control and less access to the assets and dividends which should flow these valuable resources to the provinces and to the Canadian people than is the case at present. In 1980 we were in a poorer position to take control of those assets than we were in 1970.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1981-82 SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY
speechtext: We will own the empty wells.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1981-82 SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY
speechtext:
I agree with the hon. member. The policy of saying, " we cannot afford it" is a most shortsighted one. This can be put in very simple terms. What this government is asking the Canadian people to do is to build a house on a lot they do not own. It suggests we continue to pay rent, taxes and everything else for a house on a lot we will never own.
The Liberal and Tory parties have the nerve to say to the New Democratic Party that we cannot afford Canadianiza-tion, that we cannot afford any element of public ownership. They say that is communism. It makes the most eminent, economic and basic good common sense for the Canadian people to say we can own, that we cannot afford not to own.
We are being asked to approve the borrowing of $14 billion to pay for a government policy which, in the long run, will bring virtually no benefits to the Canadian people. That is the thrust of Liberal economic policy. Let us look at the problems the Prime Minister took on in 1968 and at those which exist in 1981. The only difference is that the basic, fundamental structural problems in the economy are now worse. Nothing has been done with regard to pensions. The economic relationship between poorer Canadians and other Canadians is worse now than it was in 1968. The problem of foreign ownership is more important now. Control of the oil and gas industry is more difficult now because the value of the resource has increased. We are spending less on research and development in 1981 than we spent in 1968.
Let us examine each and every one of the fundamental problems outlined by members of the Prime Minister's party in the 1960s. Unemployment is worse now than it was in 1968. Inflation has also increased. There is not a single social and economic problem which this Prime Minister took on in 1968 that is not worse in 1981. That is the record. Now the government has the gall to come back in 1981 and ask for another $14 billion.

speechtext: You moved the motion.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1981-82 SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY
speechtext:
The hon. member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) says I moved the motion. 1 moved the motion, of
which I am extremely proud, for the simple reason that the policies being put forward by the Conservative government were exactly the same; I am not going to say they were any worse or any better.
With regard to the problems of inflation, unemployment, distribution of wealth in Canada, research and development, tell me how anything the Crosbie budget was going to do would have done anything to solve the problems we are facing.
There was also a little thing called an election which dealt with the Conservative government. That party has gone back to the couch and is determined to relive this period over and over again. I call it the pause that did not refresh, the brief interregnum of Conservative power. It was the hiccup in history. But the basic point is that neither party has been able to focus attention on the basic economic problem facing the country. Neither party has been able to speak to Canadians about the economy in a language they understand.
Economic leadership is to be able to deal compassionately with the deepest anxieties and hopes of the Canadian people. I am sorry to say that in the last 13 years we have had governments of both stripes which have demonstrated that they do not comprehend the meaning and importance of economic leadership; they do not understand the importance of the issues involved.
In order for the government to get the approval it wants from the House to borrow $14 billion, which as I said is an extremely substantial sum of money, the government must demonstrate a modicum of purpose, a modicum of intelligence, a modicum of a sense of direction, compassion and caring.
When we look not only at the structural problems facing the country, with which I have dealt to some extent, but at the human situation in which Canadians find themselves, we find that many Canadians are economically disenfranchised, are turned off and have been so abused by the political and economic processes that they do not care. They have stopped participating or believing that there is any solution to or leadership in the hopelessness of their situation.
I do not think the government deserves the approval or support of the House of Commons. One of the most fundamental, deep-seated and deep-rooted problems facing the country today is basically that we have a government which does not give a damn about jobs, inflation, food, housing or people. The fundamental malaise of Liberalism and Conservatism is that both have failed to respond to the deepest anxieties of the people. When people look to a government, whether it be provincial or federal, for an element of understanding, leadership and an ability to deal with their concerns, or when they look to Ottawa, I am sorry to say they do not find a government of which they can in any sense be proud. They do not find a government in which they have a sense that the government understands their problems and wants Canadians to take hold of their economy. They do not find a government that wants Canadians to share with one another. They do not find a
April 6, 1981

government that wants Canadians to create a humane, civilized, compassionate society.
Canadians are ready, willing and able to participate in such a society. I think Canadians want to regain control of their economy. I think Canadians feel they have been cheated because the government has failed the basic test of leadership. For those reasons we will be opposing this bill on third reading.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1981-82 SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY
speechtext:
The massive increase in investment called for by the hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood is desirable. We on this side of the House would say that the investment should be a joint one by the people of Canada through certain Crown corporations and by the private sector in the spirit of the mixed economy which has been developed over many years. I think the hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood would rather see much heavier public investment and much less private investment. But if we make this massive investment and do not increase the deficit of the federal government beyond where it is already-certainly hon. members on both sides agree that we want to see the deficit reduced-the only way to do it is by reallocating and reordering our priorities. If we reorder our priorities toward greater investment, it means that the noninvestment or consumption aspects of the federal budget must be the areas in which cuts are made.
That flies in the face of the other half of what the hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood was saying. He was saying we have to make sure that a basic social cushion is underneath Canadians so that they are not living in poverty, that senior citizens can have golden years in the true sense of the word, and that that is the area which has to be cut. There was total inconsistency in the comments made by the hon. member. I know he made them from the heart and with great emotion, but I am afraid he did not make them with great intellectual honesty, because what he is promising the people is pie in the sky, which is not possible.
The hon. member spoke only in generalities. Specifics are what we need from hon. members opposite, and there were no specifics as to how our priorities should be reordered and how funds should be made available to increase investment massively while at the same time increasing massively the social welfare system, which is a basic safety net under all Canadians. I think this House could use a lot less of that kind of speech and a lot more analytical, informed and progressive speaking on some positive examples of how these great goals can be achieved.
I was also dismayed by the cry that Canadians today are worse off than they were in 1968. An honest appraisal of the situation indicates that that is just not true in any way, shape or form. Canadians are among the best-off people on the face of the earth. I think the average Canadian understands that and is grateful. I am not saying it is the government which has brought this about, but we live in a great country which has the resources and the people to enable it to put together a society which to my mind is second to none.
The hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood said that we have higher unemployment now than we had in 1968. During the period from 1968 to today, Canada created jobs faster than any other country on the face of the earth. That is a

April 6, 1981
Borrowing Authority Act, 1981-82
statistic which is readily available to hon. members. We now have massive participation by women who have come into the labour force. Jobs have been created. More women work in the labour force now than ever in the history of Canada. More men work in the labour force now than ever in the history of the country. Our participation rate is extraordinary. It is one of the highest in the world, and we have created jobs faster than anyone else.
I agree that our inflation rate now is higher than it was in 1968. It is much higher than any of us in this House would like to see it. The government and the minister are committed to bringing that inflation down to realistic levels in the foreseeable future. That is a commitment.
The real disposable income of Canadians is higher than it has ever been. With respect to the social welfare system, the hon. member certainly chose his statistics carefully. He said that there has not been a narrowing of the gap between the rich and the poor in Canada, but on a real income basis the poor are far better off today than they were in 1968. The economic level of our whole society has been raised. The gap has not been narrowed to the extent to which perhaps some would like to see it narrowed, but certainly the well-being of Canadians is better today than it has ever been. Perhaps our expectations have not been fully realized. Perhaps we were led to expect more than our society was able to deliver in a short period of time, but certainly as a society we have achieved great things over the last 12, 15 or 20 years.

speechtext:
There are many programs which governments across the board have provided, are providing and will improve upon.
With that said, I would like to deal with the nature of the bill with which we are dealing now, Bill C-59. It deals with the request of the Government of Canada for authority from Parliament to borrow a maximum of $14 billion. This derives from the budget in which the financial requirements of the government for this coming fiscal year were forecast to be $11 billion. I certainly hope, and I am sure all of us hope, that the government is able to do even better than that and that the financial requirements will be less, but the best estimate we have is the forecast of financial requirements of $11 billion. The other $3 billion is being asked for, as I mentioned before, to provide a reserve for possible contingencies in case some unexpected shock hits the system; for example, if world oil prices were to double again, the oil import compensation payments would rise dramatically and the government would have to be in a position to cushion the shock through that program.
The second and, I think, most important aspect of that $3 billion-$3 billion added to $11 billion to make $14 billion-is a non-lapsing portion which can be carried on from fiscal year to fiscal year.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1981-82 SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY
speechtext: It will all be spent this year.

On Thursday night when I spoke, I demonstrated-quite well, I think-why that flexibility is important and should be provided to the government. Contrary to what was said by the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) on that same night, this is not an unprecedented move. In fact, this was a typical situation in previous borrowing authority bills, except for the one in 1979 introduced by the hon. member for St. John's West and the one last summer which did not have a non-lapsing feature. However, prior to that, non-lapsing features were commonplace and did provide very important flexibility for the government, as Conservative members should remember, because they ran their government for a period of seven months, without calling Parliament, on the non-lapsing authority that was available to them from previous Liberal budgets. That kind of flexibility is important. When hon. members opposite speak, I think they will agree with me that that is important.
I mentioned on Thursday night that I would try to respond to the concern which has been raised by the hon. member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) and others with regard to the current cash balances of the government and why those cash balances appear to be large. When added to the borrowing authority, they give the government a great deal of financial flexibility. I would like to say a few words about that. As the hon. member indicated, the cash balance of the government as of March 25 was $6.4 billion. Subsequently, in the last week of the month of March that sum was diminished by $1.6 billion-

-leaving $4.8 billion. There are several reasons for the current cash balance position of the government. First, there are still outstanding liabilities from the 1980-81 fiscal
April 6, 1981

year which are yet to be paid. In other words, there are cheques which are in the system which have to clear. The amounts of many of these cheques are substantial.

The hon. member says we had $1.9 billion at the end of last year, that now it is $4.8 billion and that that is a big difference. The second reason, of course, is that the cash balances of the government in the second quarter of the year will tend to be high because of the anticipated rebates of income tax; in other words, the income tax refunds which come in the first and second quarter of the calendar year, part of which lie in the previous fiscal year and part of which will lie in 1981-82 fiscal year. Those rebates come in at this time of the year and, as a result, cash balances have to be maintained at above normal levels.
Also, over the last six to nine months we have been faced with a rather precarious foreign exchange market because foreign exchange values have changed very rapidly. The Bank of Canada has been known to intervene on both sides of that market from time to time to provide some stability in that market, not trying to maintain any given level of the dollar but simply to stabilize the fluctuations in that market. That has at times required rather substantial sums. For that reason as well, the government's cash balances right now are relatively high.
Given these facts, we would expect that in the very near future the cash balances of the government will return to a more normal level and, therefore, this is a temporary aberration. The moneys that will be in the cash balance position shortly will tend to be of average size, as the hon. member opposite seems to think should be the case at this moment.

speechtext:
-because we do have these cash balances. The hon. member seems to be carrying on a debate with me. I am not sure, Mr. Speaker, which one of us has the floor. The hon. member for Mississauga South and I engage in these exchanges quite often on a friendly basis, but when one of us has the floor, I am not sure it is appropriate for the other to decide he will make more comments. I will try to restrain myself when he has the floor, if he will kindly restrain himself now that I have the floor.
I think the hon. member will see that the explanation for the cash balances which will be in the weekly statements will be that the cash balances of the government will drop down to normal levels in relatively quick order and this is not a matter which should be of significant concern to hon. members opposite. We realize that they are abnormally high at this time for the three reasons I mentioned. I assure hon. members that this is not a situation which will last and it is one that was anticipated.
In this debate on borrowing authority we have heard hon. members opposite contend that the federal government is asking for too much borrowing authority and imply at the same time that because the government has this borrowing authority it can go on a spending spree. Hon. members have contended that after Parliament has approved this borrowing authority there will be no checks on government spending, that the government can simply borrow all of that $14 billion and spend and spend. Well, Mr. Speaker, I think that is doing a disservice to the Canadian public and it is certainly doing a disservice to the people who are watching us on television.
Also, it is being somewhat dishonest or ignorant, and I am not sure exactly which, because the Canadian federal Financial system is such that that simply is not possible, and hon. members opposite know that. The government, of whatever political stripe it may be, brings forward during the year its estimates which lay out a spending program reflecting the fiscal statement of the minister in his budget. The estimates reflect the expenditure plans of each and every department, and supplementary estimates are brought down when they are needed. The main point is that in every case the main estimates and the supplementary estimates which constrain the spending of government and of every department and agency in government are approved by Parliament. Parliamentarians in this House and in committee scrutinize and approve every dime that is spent by the government. So if those estimates do not show spending above $11 billion or $12 billion in the next year-in this case, the total budget is in the range of $65 billion, if that is the spending level that is approved by Parliament in the estimates-then that is what the government is constrained to spend. It cannot spend any more unless it comes back to Parliament to get further approval.
We have admitted, and hon. members have noted, that the borrowing authority for which we are asking is $14 billion, even though our financial forecasts show that the shortfall between our revenues and our expenditures will be only $11 billion. There is no way that that extra $3 billion-if we are successful in holding down expenditures even further, there

April 6, 1981
Borrowing Authority Act, 1981-82
will be an excess of $4 billion or $5 billion-will be used frivolously by the government without coming back to Parliament and laying before Parliament its plans for that expenditure. There are controls and constraints on the level of government spending, on what those moneys are spent, and of course there are constraints on the amount that the government can borrow. What we are talking about in this bill is parliamentary approval for the borrowing that will be necessary to meet the approved expenditures which the government has put forward to Parliament.
I suggest that when the hon. member for Broadview-Green-wood and others say that the government's spending priorities are out of line, that is a charge that should be raised and carefully scrutinized when we start looking at the estimates of the department and in what areas hon. members would like to see expenditures reduced, so that perhaps some of the lofty goals to which the hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood referred could, in fact, be realized.
I think it must be made clear to the people that there are constraints on the government's expenditures and borrowing, and that those constraints are imposed by Parliament, so there is no way the government can exceed the limit without further parliamentary approval. The government is not, as some hon. members opposite have indicated, asking for a blank cheque, since in the Canadian parliamentary system there is no such thing as a blank cheque. If the hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood was here, I would say that there is no such thing as a free lunch either; but that would only make him feel good.
To summarize, I would like to say that the minister started his tenure with a financial statement as to what he believed the future held for the economy. He followed that up with a budget, which for the first time laid out in an envelope the expenditures of the government, the expected revenues, the financial requirements, what will have to be borrowed to make up the difference, a planned gradual reduction in the deficit and an improvement in the spending priorities of the government under the envelope system which was brought down. We examined, debated and voted on that budget.
After that we had the estimates which take our expenditure plans down to the most minute detail. I might say in passing that the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston) has just brought down a plan which will make the estimates even more useful to hon. members in scrutinizing government expenditures. I think this is a great step forward and I congratulate the President of the Treasury Board for bringing down these measures. I have just seen a report which has been tabled by the President of the Treasury Board with respect to the Lambert commission, which report will improve the operations of the government even more.
The government is working very diligently on improving the efficiency and effectiveness of its operations. It is helping the Canadian people get far more value for the money which is made available to the government to spend on the public's behalf. We now have a complete description of where the
money will be spent and a request in Bill C-59 for the additional funds which will be necessary to finance those expenditures. Given that we now have this measure before us, we would all very much like to see a lesser amount being requested in the borrowing authority, as the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) and the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Bussieres) have indicated. We would like to have a lower deficit and more growth in the economy. Those are common goals which we all share.
A realistic assessment of the situation indicates that the sum requested is what will be required to do the job. I realize that we would all like to have something better, but when you face the facts, which is what the Minister of Finance must do, then you must ask yourself, "What is my realistic assessment of what I will have to borrow in the marketplace to meet the expenditures which have been approved by Parliament?" That is the amount we are asking for in the borrowing authority bill, with the addition of the amount I have indicated for flexibility, which will not be used unless the government returns to Parliament to ask for additional spending authority.
All rhetoric aside, the bill before us asks for what is realistically required. Yes, we want to reduce that requirement in the future. Yes, the minister has put forward a plan for reducing those financial requirements, reducing the deficit and enhancing the over-all accountability, efficiency and effectiveness of government over the next few years. I think this is a realistic plan. It is one which hon. members on both sides of the House should accept and approve, given that they have already approved the expenditure plan that is to be financed by this particular piece of legislation.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, Bill C-59 is a very important bill. It asks the Parliament of Canada to approve $14 billion in borrowing-

As I was just about to say, all on one page and a bit. The amount of $14 billion is approximately five times the total budget of the province in which I live.
This bill is also important because borrowing has come to be a larger part of the government's expenditure. This can be looked at in several ways. In the past it has been pointed out that present government borrowing amounts to more than the total budget of the Government of Canada some 12 years ago. It has also been pointed out that in those 12 years our national deficit has amounted to a sum so large that the interest charged against it each year exceeds the total amount of money spent by the government some 12 years ago. It is an extremely large amount of money. As has been said previously, it accounts for something in the range of 19 per cent of total government expenditure.
I like to look at it in another way. It means that out of each dollar of taxes collected on behalf of the Government of Canada, some 25 cents is used to pay interest on past government debt. I am sorry that the hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood (Mr. Rae) did not stay to listen to the debate. I
April 6, 1981

think too many times this is what the NDP does. They do not really care what goes on in the House; they make speeches and run out to make the best possible use of the press that they can.

speechtext: It seems to me, for whatever reason, members of the NDP use the House as little as possible. The critic for the New Democratic Party, once he makes his speech, could at least stay in the House and listen to what goes on. The hon. member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) is our spokesman on this bill. He has been in the House, participated in the debate-

speechtext: He does not get invited to make speeches outside.
