speechtext:
It is amazing to me that anyone would want to listen to them, but I guess it takes all kinds.
One of the points that the hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood made-and I will refer to him again, if I may, without upsetting my friends to my left, which is where they should be, to my left-was that he found it unfortunate that the government was borrowing money simply to pay for groceries. I think he should have gone further. I think what disturbs many of us on this side of the House is that the government is borrowing money to pay for yesterday's groceries, which is even worse.
The hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood wondered why it was all right for Noranda to be involved in takeovers and why we were being critical of the Government of Canada with respect to takeovers. There is a very simple explanation. We are here as elected representatives and we are voicing our concerns on behalf of the taxpayers of Canada who, in a very real sense, are the shareholders on behalf of the Government of Canada. If we do not have an opportunity to stand up and question some of the expenditures that the Government of Canada makes on behalf of its citizens, then no one else will. It seems to me that if the hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood wanted to be consistent, he would have gone further in his analogy and said that none of the shareholders in Noranda should have been concerned about any of the things that Noranda does on their behalf. I am sure that that would not be the case. The next time there is an annual meeting of the shareholders of Noranda, they will be questioning the takeover procedures and the money that was spent on behalf of the shareholders. At that meeting there will have to be some accountability given for the actions of the directors in the past.
Borrowing Authority Act, 1981-82
That is precisely what should happen in the House of Commons.
To pursue the matter further, if the people who have bought shares in Noranda are unhappy or if, for some reason, they think the directors have done things which are wrong and the shares of Noranda fall in value, the shareholders are in a position where they can sell the shares of that particular company. However, the taxpayers of Canada cannot do that, unfortunately; when the government makes bad commitments on behalf of its citizens, the taxpayers cannot get out and sell their shares in the country. It is incumbent on all of us who are elected to represent our constituents that we question the spending practices of this government. It is then an entirely understandable concept; and I find it unfortunate that the spokesman for the NDP, on behalf of the finance department, cannot see and make that very simple distinction.
There are many things that the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Evans) said and to which I would like to make reference. However, I will just mention a few. He mentioned that we should somehow reorder our specifics. He pointed to the fact that the NDP has been inconsistent too often, and that, by implication, we in this party have been inconsistent in that, while asking for increased government expenditure, we also wail away and complain that the government deficit increases. While that does happen I, for one, have not made those kinds of suggestions. I think that many of us who are interested in the financial affairs of this country on behalf of our party have tried to be consistent and have not asked for increased government involvement in government programs while complaining about increasing deficits.
That brings me to some of the concerns that I have with the bill. I do not see anything wrong at all with the government's coming to Parliament and asking for the authority to borrow more money. I think it is an entirely legitimate activity to be engaged in. However, what I do object to-and I think it is a legitimate objection-is the fact that we are being asked to give authority to the government to borrow $3 billion as a contingency.
The parliamentary secretary said, rightly so, that the Parliament of Canada scrutinizes the estimates. If it wants to spend an additional $3 billion, the Government of Canada must come back with supplementary estimates to ask for authority to spend this $3 billion.
Given that fact, I see nothing wrong with the intent of the amendment of my colleague the hon. member for Mississauga South that we not give the government this contingency borrowing authority. If it is necessary to come back with supplementary estimates to spend the $3 billion, I see nothing wrong with the government's coming back to Parliament for additional borrowing authority at the same time. In that way we who take ourselves seriously as legislators and try to do the best we can on behalf of our constituents would then be in a position at the same time to examine supplementary estimates, vote, and

April 6, 1981
Borrowing Authority Act, 1981-82 give the government authority for the additional $3 billion that it claims it needs for contingencies.
The parliamentary secretary said that one of the reasons the government may require the additional $3 billion is that world oil prices could double. Heaven forbid that we should get ourselves into that kind of a scenario. However, I think that points out some of the problems that the government has gotten itself into, because it has not developed secure Canadian supplies which would be more predictable in their price.
We can see the folly of the National Energy Program as it is presently being used by the government. In fact, it is not encouraging increases in domestic supply. If anything, it is discouraging Canadians from developing their own sources of supply, and not only conventional crude. We have seen the cutbacks in production from the province of Alberta. We have seen that heavy oil and tar sands plants have not gone ahead, and in some cases are as much as two years behind schedule. If the government was serious about making the country self-sufficient in energy, it would have gone ahead and reached a price agreement so that we could be in a position to be more self-reliant with our own supplies of oil. If that is one of the contingencies for which the government needs to borrow the $3 billion, I submit that if it would spend more attention and time on developing our own sources of supply it would probably not need that kind of money for that kind of contingency. 1 find it unfortunate that this type of contingency is considered in additional government spending.
One of the other interesting phrases that the parliamentary secretary used was to call a surplus of money-I think, $4 billion or $5 billion-a "temporary aberration". I would think that that is exactly what it is, based on the spending habits of this government. It is unfortunate that because of past spending habits, and because we have been in the hole, we look at a surplus position as being a temporary aberration. That gives us an idea of the attitude of the government to spending the dollars of taxpayers.
The parliamentary secretary referred to "putting all rhetoric aside", and then he went on to say that the government should be accountable, it should be efficient, and it should be- another four or five-syllable word; I cannot make out my own writing here. However, it seems to me that if we are going to put all rhetoric aside, we should talk in simple, straightforward and honest terms and not get into these long four or five-syllable words. I would be very happy to see the government put rhetoric aside and get down to brass tacks in considering government spending.
My hon. colleague the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor) talks about bread and butter issues. That is what we understand in this country, and that is what has made this country great. Bread and butter issues will make this country great again if those issues are allowed to make gain of some importance in the future.
I would like to talk about how I believe the massive borrowing that the government has been engaged in for the past number of years has affected the farming communities in the country. We all know that, by and large, the farmers in this
country serve the citizens as well as any country in the world, because we spend on food a smaller proportion of our take home pay-our gross national product, for that matter, too- as individual citizens who feed ourselves, than any other country in the world with the exception of the United States, and we run a very close second to the Americans. We spend something like 18 per cent of our disposable income on food. This also takes into account the fact that we eat something like 40 per cent of our meals away from home. That tells me that the agricultural industry in this country has served the people of Canada very well.
To give an example, there is now a saying that it will not be very long before the potato will not go into a modern kitchen unless it has somehow been prepared, is already peeled and baked for the consumer, for the homemaker, because we have come a long way from the time when we simply bought potatoes in stores, brought them home and cooked them. A very large percentage of potatoes eaten in Canadian homes are now prepared or pre-processed in some way.
What has happened is that, in order for the farmers to be this productive, they have had to make use of very large amounts of capital so that the amount of capital required to create a job in the agricultural industry in this country is larger than in any other industry. What happens when the government gets involved, the way it is, in borrowing large amounts of money is that there are strains on individual farming operations in terms of their ability to borrow at reasonable interest rates, and this drives up the interest rate.
I can give some examples, and I have three ways of looking at it. I took the figures from the Bank of Canada Review. The total borrowing-this is non-equity security borrowings in Canada-for the calendar year 1980 was $21.8 billion. Of that amount, $11.4 billion was borrowed by the federal government, and it accounts for 52.2 per cent. Over half the nonequitable securities issued in Canada were taken up by the federal government. The provinces accounted for $7.7 billion, and the municipalities accounted for $.6 billion. Out of the figure I have quoted of $21.8 billion, approximately 90 per cent was borrowed by three levels of government.
It is no wonder that we see interest rates on loans to farmers increase. The three levels of government have become such large borrowers that there is a limited amount of money available for the private sector, and when the private sector goes to the market, it finds interest rates have been driven up by the activities of the three levels of government.
I have an article from The Globe and Mail, dated November 18 which points out that:
Federal financing of $8.19 billion accounted for 41 per cent of the nine-month total. Provincial and agency borrowing amounted to $3.73 billion (19 per cent of the total). Municipalities raised $1.06 billion (5 per cent).
This set of statistics includes borrowings made out of the country. Previously when we looked at borrowings within the country only, the three levels of government accounted for something like 90 per cent of the total. If we include borrowings from outside the country, then the three levels of governments account for 65 per cent of the total. It seems to me when
April 6, 1981

the government is involved as heavily as it is in the capital market, that leaves precious little money with which private industry can operate.
Another way of looking at the federal government deficit is in terms of percentage of the gross national product. I have in front of me a recent issue of the pamphlet Business Review issued by the Bank of Montreal, for February, 1981. It contains a graph which shows that in 1978 the federal government deficit, shown as a percentage of the gross national product, came to almost 5 per cent. In 1979, when this party formed the government, so we can take some of the credit or blame, the figure dropped to about 3.4 per cent of the gross national product. Last year, with the Liberals back in power, it reached 4.2 per cent. It is evident that when this government is involved, the borrowing, as a percentage of the gross national product, becomes too large and this does not leave enough money to enable the private sector to borrow at reasonable rates.
The hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood pointed out that there are different types of borrowings in which we may become involved. Whether we are farmers, whether we run a household or a small business, I think we all know it is possible to borrow money for investment so that the investment will return the initial amount of money borrowed. If the borrowing is for capital projects, it would not make any difference whether we borrow the money outside Canada, from individuals, or from banks; as long as the money regenerates itself, we would be in a position to pay it back. Once the money was paid back, then the facility or whatever was established would be there, creating jobs and wealth in the country.
In too many instances, that has not been the case where this government is concerned, however, and that is why we ask that they give some indication of the purpose of the borrowing. The parliamentary secretary objected to the use of the words "blank cheque" but, in effect, the request for $3 billion is a request for a blank cheque because we have not seen the supplementary estimates to establish that the government needs to spend that money. If we were sure the money was to be spent on capital projects which would make the country more productive, then I am sure we would agree that the money should be borrowed. We hav- not been given that indication, however. The examination cf estimates in committee is often a very frustrating, time-consuming and non-productive exercise. I think we would all agree that this examination is not adequate in view of the amount of money we are being asked to approve on behalf of our constituents.
If the money borrowed were spent on capital projects which would finance themselves, then it would not make a great deal of difference who it was borrowed from because we would be in a position to repay it from the earnings. That is not the kind of borrowing this government is asking the Parliament of Canada to approve, however.
It is interesting to note that amount of interest on past government debt, which is to be paid this year, is about the
Borrowing Authority Act, 1981-82
same as the amount we are being asked to approve in this borrowing bill. This reminds me of a statement by John Stuart Mill, the famous economist, who said something to the effect that you cannot make a storekeeper rich by stealing from him and then using the money to buy goods from his store. It seems to me this is the kind of situation the government is in now; it borrows money to pay for yesterday's groceries and then, in returning the interest payment to the taxpayer, it turns around and taxes the taxpayer on the interest it is paying back to him and recovers the money in that way.
I do not think we can speak about generating wealth in the country unless we are planning to spend some of the borrowings we are being asked to approve on some legitimate capital projects.
I would go further, Mr. Speaker. Three or four weeks ago the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston) tabled his estimates in this House. We all know the procedural hassle we got into then. I had the opportunity to ask him if there was any provision in the estimates for the western development fund. He pointed out that there was a provision in the estimates for spending $350 million of the $4 billion which had been promised in the throne speech. He did not indicate where the money would be spent. Several members from western Canada suggested it should be spent on capital projects which would make that part of the country more productive. At that time, however, there was no indication how the $350 million was to be spent.
Questions put to the minister when he tabled the estimates and further questions put to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) in committee brought forth no indication that guidelines had been set for spending the money. That belies some of the points made by the parliamentary secretary about the necessity of having the estimates approved in the House before the money is spent. When we on this side of the House attempt to find out in committee what the government's spending plans are, we do not receive adequate answers.
I do not think farmers and operators of small businesses are very different, Mr. Speaker; they operate on six, eight, or nine-month production periods. This is particularly so in the cattle business. A farmer has to commit himself to buying feeder cattle which will be fed over a period of six or eight months. In that time-span, interest rates may go through the roof to a point where it would cost in the neighbourhood of 20 cents per pound to put a finished animal in position to be slaughtered and show up as meat on a supermarket counter. At today's prices, that 20 cents per pound is 25 per cent or 30 per cent of the total market value of the animal. Faced with that kind of arithmetic when deciding whether to produce additional beef, buy additional cattle or put the grain through livestock as a marketing tool, a lot of producers have already decided against it, and in fact have cut back on the number of animals available for slaughter. This has a negative effect on the supply of beef.
High interest rates discourage cattle producers from making additional supplies available to the consumer. We all know that as supplies contract, prices go up. That hurts the very

April 6, 1981
Borrowing Authority Act, 1981-82 process which the government is trying to make work in this time of inflation. It holds down the money supply and drives up interest rates. As I pointed out, as interest rates go up in the beef business, that hurts the supply of cattle. The whole exercise has exactly the opposite effect to that which the government and the Bank of Canada would like.
Last week the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) announced an increase in the Farm Credit Corporation interest rates from 12.75 per cent to 14 per cent, an all-time high. I fail to see how an increase in the interest rate will help inflation. Instead, it will drive producers out of business and the supply of products to the consumer will decrease. In turn, this will drive up the price.
One of the things that disturbs many people in western Canada is the way our transportation system for grain is being taxed to the limit. This will have an adverse effect on the movement of all the products we are capable of producing in western Canada to an export position. It applies to bulk commodities which are in demand around the world; sulphur, potash, grain and coal. In the past year we have heard a lot in this House and in the country about the Crow rate. This is a very emotional issue because it is an historical rate in western Canada. Some people claim it should not be touched, while others say it should be abolished.
I think everyone agrees that the railways are not deriving enough revenue from the movement of grain to cover the actual moving costs. There is a separate argument as to how much loss of revenue the railways are suffering. Some people say the actual charge is only covering one fifth of the cost of moving grain; some say it is more like one third. Others argue that the railways are being compensated adequately, but most people agree the railways are not receiving enough revenue from the movement of grain to cover the actual costs incurred.
Unless some solution is reached quite quickly on this impasse, then the railways will not be in a position to move all the bulk commodities we will have for export in western Canada two or three years hence. I think most people would feel comfortable if the Government of Canada were borrowing money for capital improvements to the railways.
I know the railways would much rather see an increase in the rates they charge in order to generate their own revenues to spend on their capital projects. I think it is incumbent on the government to show some leadership in this important issue. If it does not, we will find ourselves unable to earn the kind of foreign exchange of which we are capable. We know that the more we export, the more foreign exchange we earn. This results in less pressure on the Canadian dollar. As well, the Bank of Canada would be able to lower interest rates, benefiting everyone. The government of the day would not have to come to Parliament to ask for as much money as it is now, because Canada would be earning more money on foreign exchange and that money would find its way into the economy through what is called a multiplier effect. More taxes would be generated and the whole country would benefit. On behalf of
the people in my region I want to say that this is an area in which I would like to see some leadership and emphasis. We will then be in a position to contribute, not only for our own region but for the whole country.
I have one more concern. It deals with the way the Bank of Canada operates in this country. As we all know, the Bank of Canada has become a very large part of our financial lives. In the annual report of the Governor of the Bank of Canada to the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen), we find this statement:
The responsibility of the bank is to discharge its Parliamentary mandate "to regulate credit and currency in the best interests of the economic life of the nation".
The phrase in quotes is from the act. The responsibility for the bank is a very large responsibility and one which I am sure everyone involved with the Bank of Canada takes very seriously. I think one can make the argument that the Bank of Canada today has in some instances much more to do with our economic life than the Minister of Finance. I find this unfortunate in some ways because the Minister of Finance is accountable to the House of Commons and, therefore, to those of us who are elected to represent our constituents. Yet the Bank of Canada, through its board of directors, makes some very important decisions on our behalf almost every day of every week. I suspect very few Canadians know who serves on their board of directors. These people determine at what level the money supply will be increased. They determine, in effect, by regulating the amount of negotiable securities put on the market each Thursday of every week by the Bank of Canada at the treasury bill auction, the interest rate that chartered banks charge.
As a matter of interest, I would like to read into the record the names of those who serve on the board of directors of the Bank of Canada. I think it is important that all Canadians know who these people are. The Governor of the Bank of Canada is Mr. Gerald K. Bouey; the deputy governor is Mr. R. William Lawson. The governor and the deputy governor are both full-time directors. They spend all of their time on issues relating to the Bank of Canada. There are 12 directors who work on a part-time basis. They are as follows: Robert W. Campbell, Calgary, Alberta; William Dodge, Ottawa, Ontario; D. Michael M. Goldie, Vancouver, British Columbia; Sol Kanee, Winnipeg, Manitoba; Spencer G. Lake, Ramea, New-foudland; Alie A. LeBouthillier, Caraquet, New Brunswick; J. William E. Mingo, Halifax, Nova Scotia; Mrs. Yseult Lefebvre-Richard, Montreal, P.Q.; Joseph H. Potts, Toronto, Ontario; Donald Smith, Charlottetown, P.E.I.; John A. Stack, Saskatoon, Saskatchewan, and Jacques Taschereau, Quebec, P.Q.
I am sure few Canadians know very much about the fourteen people, I have just listed or know much about their business backgrounds. Yet a very good case could be made that they have as much to do with the monetary and fiscal policy of this government as the Minister of Finance. In my opinion, I do not think this composition should be allowed to continue. I would be in favour of seeing the addition of two
April 6, 1981

Members of Parliament to the board of directors of the Bank of Canada, not necessarily because they should have a lot of input and should make drastic changes, but simply so they could have a better understanding and could have some input when the occasion arises in terms of the way the Bank of Canada is administering the monetary policy in this country. As I have said, monetary policy is very important. Anyone who thinks otherwise has only to look at the level of interest rates we have experienced for the last year to realize that it is extremely important.
I hope the day comes when we do have Members of Parliament on the board of directors of the Bank of Canada. I do not believe it would make the board unduly political. On the contrary, I think it would make it much more responsive and accountable to the people of Canada for whom it is set up to serve. In addition, it would go a long way to seeing that the Bank of Canada does in fact regulate credit and currency in the best interests of the economic life of this nation.
I find it unfortunate that the government is asking for so much money in the form of the borrowing authority. I see nothing wrong with the government accepting the amendment moved by my colleague, the hon. member for Mississauga South to the effect that if the government does need supplementary borrowing authority it can come back to the House. We should not be in the position of voting to give the government blanket authority for an additional $3 billion after the beginning of its next fiscal year in April, 1982. I will have no trouble at all, in fact, my conscience will not allow me to do anything different than to vote against this bill.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1981-82 SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the suggestions made from the other side that the government should come back more often, and that we should have smaller borrowing bills is perhaps desirable. The problem is that we have a lot of business to deal with in the course of a year in this House of Commons. If the government came back twice as often, we would have a lot less time to do a lot of other things. What has been going on in this House during the last few weeks is a good example of how House time is used up, in what I term a disreputable sort of way, and how we are unable to get on with the business of the House.
It seems to me that members opposite always want to spend more time doing this and more time doing that. If we did not bring in such things as closure, we would not be able to manage the country, nor could we get the business of the House done. If there were some evidence that we could have a smaller borrowing bill and get it through in one or two sessions of the House, it might be possible, but the constant necessity of bringing in closure is caused basically by the fact that we cannot seem to move things in the House.
On Friday last, I spoke on the borrowing bill at report stage. I had only 20 minutes and I did not finish everything I wanted to say. Today I would like to go somewhat further, but first I want to review some of the comments I made earlier. I will then approach the fiscal powers of the federal and provincial governments which I think are the keys to the whole surplus-deficit situation.
Borrowing Authority Act, 1981-82
First, the reason for borrowing, that is the debt, can only be expressed in an intelligent manner when related to the gross national product. It does not make sense to talk about personal debt as an absolute number. For example, I may owe $10,000. That does not mean anything unless I relate it to my income. If my income is $100,000, the $10,000 is manageable. If my income is $ 10,000, it is a lot less manageable.
The same can be said about the net national debt as a function of the gross national product. Most of these matters have to be measured in that fashion. Whether the gross national product is a relatively small amount or is, as it is today, close to $300 billion, that has a very definite effect on the amount of money that can be borrowed.
In 1951, we talked about the net national debt being 50 per cent of the gross national product. That was very meaningful. It was not expressed in absolute terms. In 1981 the national debt as a function of the GNP is around 30 per cent. I will not go into that in detail, but it is important. We should relate these things, and the GNP is a simple way of doing it.
I looked at government expenditures on which this borrowing is based. Transfers to the provinces, to people and to corporations in terms of subsidies amounted to 48.9 per cent, almost 50 per cent of all federal government spending. Payments of the public debt came to 19 per cent. Transfers to people and provinces, including those who hold government bonds or have loaned money to the federal government, such as banks, totalled 68 per cent of all government spending. The cost of operating the government is 32 per cent; basically the cost of subsidies to Crown corporations, running the RCMP, the military, post office and so on. The 68 per cent is the transfer portion.
A lot has been said about cutting the fat from government expenditures. That must come out of the 31 per cent. There is obviously some fat, but it cannot be cut in any significant way. If we want to seriously cut back, it must be from the 68 per cent.
What concerns me today is the transfers to the provinces. Straight dollar transfers and tax point transfers are in the order of $18.9 billion, or 28 per cent of the $67.5 billion government expenditure. In other words, 28 per cent of federal government expenditures is transferred to the provinces and municipalities. The sum is transferred directly to the provinces and then to the municipalities, and a relatively small amount direct to the municipalities. It is that very large transfer that is getting us into trouble.
When we talk about the borrowing bill, we get to the heart of what the whole Constitution business is all about. We have to face up to the federal-provincial fiscal arrangements. On Friday I referred to the way governments have grown. I stated that in 1943, in the height of World War II, the federal government revenues were 22.3 per cent of the GNP and 3.3 per cent for the provinces. If we include municipalities, it would probably raise the figure to 5 per cent or 6 per cent. By 1960, the federal portion of the GNP in revenue terms was 17

April 6, 1981
Borrowing Authority Act, 1981-82
per cent and 6.1 per cent for the provinces. In 1970 the federal portion was 16.1 per cent and the provinces 12.3 per cent. In 1979, the last year for which I have figures, the federal portion was down to 16.6 per cent and the provincial portion up to 15 per cent.
Since World War II, there has been a decline from 22.3 per cent to 16.6 per cent. Since 1970 there has been a decline from 17 per cent to 16.6 per cent. In that same period, provincial revenues increased from 6.1 per cent to 15 per cent of the GNP, a tremendous growth in the provincial share.
I think it is worth making a comparison with the United States. I will do this on an expenditure basis because I only have approximations for revenue. Federal government expenditures in the United States represent 60 per cent of all government expenditures in that federal union. State and municipal expenditures represent 40 per cent.
Some on this side are very strong proponents of provincial rights and others of federal rights. I am a strong proponent of the federal government having more power. In Canada, federal government expenditures represent 45 per cent of all government expenditures, and the provinces and municipalities represent 55 per cent. We have a very interesting concept. Which is the more powerful? In the United States it is 60-40 federal, state and municipal, and in Canada it is 45-55.
May I call it six o'clock.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before I launch into the basis of my speech on third reading of the borrowing authority bill, I should like to make one last point. It concerns government expenditures on goods and services. Many economists would look at government expenditures in two ways. One way would be to look at goods and services and then the balance, which would basically be transfers.
Looking at the goods and services side and speaking in relation to the gross national product-and this is information taken from a book entitled "Unemployment and Inflation" by Barber and McCallum-in 1953 we find that the total federal expenditure in fixed dollars declined from 10 per cent of the gross national product to about 6 per cent in 1978. This is really what the federal government absorbs; it is not the transfers, which would be the balance. This includes federal defence and non-defence spending. So, there was an actual decline in what the government takes out of the economy.
Basically we find the opposite situation in the provinces. The provinces absorbed something like 6 per cent in 1953. This rose to about 10 per cent or 11 per cent in 1979. When one
adds in the local governments and hospitals, it rises from approximately 10 per cent to 15 per cent, 16 per cent or 17 per cent.
This business about government spending being the main cause of inflation is highly distorted, when one considers that the federal government's share of goods and services has declined significantly since 1953; there has been a steady decline.
I should like to go back to the real crunch of the constitutional debate, that is, the second phase; where we are going and why we are doing it. It has a great deal to do with the fiscal arrangements between the provinces and the federal government. Previously I indicated there was a very large growth in provincial revenues relative to federal revenues. In 1960 the federal government revenue was 17 per cent of the gross national product and the revenue of the provincial governments was approximately 6.1 per cent. In 1979, the latest year for which I have figures, it was roughly 16.6 per cent to 15.5 per cent. Then I indicated that 60 per cent of all government expenditures in the United States was by the federal government and that 40 per cent was by the states and municipalities. In Canada it was 45 per cent federal and 55 per cent provincial and municipal. If fiscal power is what counts, then the American federal government is much stronger than we are. If we turn to the revenue side, the federal government's revenue is about 40 per cent and the provinces' and municipalities' is about 60 per cent. We have this particular problem.
I should like to go back and deal with the fiscal history of the country very briefly. I heard some speakers on the other side who did not realize that the Fathers of Confederation looked at the American system when they were setting up this country. At the time they indicated that the American system was not working and that they wanted a much stronger federal government. This is what Macdonald and Brown were concerned about. They set up a fiscal system which gave the federal government a lot of power. In those days indirect taxation, customs duties and so on were the major sources of government revenue. They considered this to be a prime system.
Actually, from 1867 to around 1914, and even later, there was a great decline in the fiscal power of the federal government. It was not what Macdonald and others had expected. Then World War I increased federal government power. There was a much greater increase in provincial power between 1919 and 1930. Then the provinces almost collapsed. They reached their heights and then collapsed; bankruptcy was avoided by federal government assistance. Then there was a growing increase of federal government power during the 1930s and the period of World War II. Afterwards there was a recession in federal power and a growth in the power of the provinces and the municipalities in terms of fiscal arrangements.
Now we have a situation which is extremely acute. I should like to talk about surpluses and deficits. Today the federal deficit is approximately $15 billion. I should like to refer to the
April 6, 1981

annual review entitled "a climate of uncertainty" of the Economic Council of Canada.
Looking at this chart we see a deficit which continues right through the eighties and into 1990, perhaps slightly less in terms of gross national product, but we see the opposite situation with the provinces and municipalities which move well into a surplus situation. This is particularly so with respect to the province of Alberta, but also to some extent in the other two western resource-rich provinces. However, there is a basic surplus at that stage of the game. If we put all levels of government together, as the Economic Council of Canada has done, we see that by about 1984 all governments have a zero surplus and a zero deficit, and then as we go on for another year or two we find that all governments have surpluses, except the federal government, which has a very large deficit. This will create some very serious problems in this country. The problems will become greater as the resource revenues, particularly of Alberta, increase.
I was appalled this past weekend to hear the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) say that Alberta need only hang tough to win the energy pricing fight. To Alberta he said, "Stand firm". Alberta is trying to raise the price of energy from $17 or $18 a barrel to about $32 a barrel. I calculate that the hon. member who was responsible for that 18-cent budget would like another 43 cents added to the cost of each gallon of gasoline. I suppose that is what he was talking about. Do hon. members know what that means in terms of inflation? It means about a 4 per cent or 5 per cent increase in inflation. That is not just an increase for a short period; it is an increase forever. When hon. members are talking about these things, they should remember that our constituents back home are not particularly happy about that. My constituents in Thunder Bay would not be very happy to see another 45 cents added to the cost of a gallon of gasoline. They are not anxious to see a 4 per cent to 5 per cent increase in inflation. That is what the hon. member was talking about, but he was also talking about a massive transfer to one province, which basically means that the wealth of that province-or other provinces; perhaps one, two or three-will increase while at the same time we continue with this very large federal deficit.
I think the real issues this nation will face in the next five or ten years will be energy and inflation, but at the heart of them will be the very basic problem of the fiscal arrangements between the provinces and the federal government. I think we as a federal government must maintain a firm hand in this matter.
Let us examine some of the arrangements we have with the provinces. Let us examine medicare, for instance. Six years ago the federal government put up 44 per cent or 45 per cent of all of the medical costs in the province of Ontario, and the province and the individuals who paid premiums were putting up the balance. Something is happening to that arrangement. Something has happened over the years. The federal government is now paying 50 per cent of this, and Ontario is
Borrowing Authority Act, 1981-82
supposed to be a "have" province. The share of the province of Ontario is down to about 30 per cent, and the individual users of the service pay the premiums, which make up another 20 per cent.
There is a special task force on federal-provincial fiscal arrangements, but if in the next few years we decide that the federal government has to cut back then can we be sure the services this country has come to expect-medicare and so forth-will continue to be provided and can we be assured that the provinces will keep their part up if we cut back our share to perhaps where it was? I do not think we can because many of the provinces have not shown themselves to be honest or forthright in maintaining these services.
When we come to deciding whether we should increase federal revenues or cut back federal expenditures in terms of cutting off some of these services, I think we must look to see whether these services can be continued by the provinces. If we feel, as I think I would, given the evidence before me today, that these provinces will not maintain these services, then I think I would have to opt for an increase in federal revenues in some way so we can be sure someone is maintaining the services that we believe all Canadians should have, and some of the areas where we will find those revenues happen to be in resource areas where there is this tremendous transfer.
I am not anticipating what all our reactions will be, but I am saying these are the issues which must be put before this House. These are the issues which are really germane to the constitutional issue. It seems to me there has been a growing increase in the fiscal power of the provinces. It seems to me that as a nation, we have come to the point where we have to start turning that around so the federal government has sufficient power and sufficient fiscal resources to do the job Canadians expect to be done.

Mr. Speaker, it is a great pleasure to listen to the hon. member for Thunder Bay-Atikokan (Mr. McRae). This is the second time he has given the same speech in two business days in this House. I enjoyed listening to it last Friday. It was not too bad today. I hope he will not give the same speech again the next time he stands up.
The hon. member for Thunder Bay-Atikokan is a gentleman who proclaims that hon. members opposite should rule with a firm hand. I do not know whether they have a firm hand, but I can say they surely have sticky fingers.
The whole proposition the hon. member put before us can be torn to pieces in just a few short sentences. The hon. member pointed out that at the time of the Second World War a certain percentage of the gross national product represented federal government expenditures. It seems strange to me that at that time Canada was able to fight a major world war with probably a smaller proportion of the gross national product of the country than what is used now just to keep the normal functions of government going.
The hon. member made a comparison of the national debt of this country in terms of the percentage of the gross national

April 6, 1981
Borrowing Authority Act, 1981-82
product. It is quite right to point out that since the end of the last world war this has consistently gone down. That is right, it went down in fact until about 1968 when the present Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) took office and then, instead of continuing to go down or levelling off as one might expect- because it is quite natural that it should be very, very high, in wartime, and one would expect that 20 or 25 years after it would reach a steady levelling off-this has not happened in the last 12 years or so. It dipped, and now it is climbing up again. We are not fighting a war. We are not engaged in any major capital expenditures or any major public works projects in this country. All we are doing is running faster and faster on the same treadmill.
The hon. member says, and it is true, that provincial expenditures have increased considerably compared with federal government expenditures. But at the same time we must look into the nature of provincial type expenditures. We must remember that prior to the Second World War, expenditures on health services, education and social services by federal or provincial governments were pretty limited. They were normally the responsibility of a parish or of a local school district, and it was not required of any provincial or federal government to expend money on that type of activity. What has happened over the last 30 years or so? In the last 30 years or so, government expenditures for health, welfare and education grew so much that now it is probably the biggest area of total government spending. Because that is primarily an area of provincial authority, the provincial share of total government expenditures has had to rise during that period. I do not think it is a nefarious plot on the part of the provinces. Rather, it has occurred naturally. The people of Canada have wanted government at one level or another to engage in this type of social expenditures.
I would now like to get back to the bill before us, namely, Bill C-59, which would authorize the borrowing of $14 billion. It is a pleasure for me to be able to speak on this subject tonight instead of continuing the debate on the Constitution. I am pleased that a truce, as the newspapers have called it, took place a couple of days ago. I am glad hon. members opposite have dropped their obsession with this matter for a limited period of time, and I would like to urge them to drop the constitutional issue for another couple of weeks or so to allow us to take a breather. We could then come back and take another look at the issue after some things have a chance to happen in the next couple of days. There is the Quebec provincial election, for instance, which is to take place in a few days. It seems that the premiers at long last have been able to get their act together. It would be my idea to let the constitutional issue lie for a few weeks so that we could come back to it with fresh minds.

speechtext:
Let us get back now to the borrowing authority for $14 billion requested of us by the government. In my estimation, this comes to about $700 from every man, woman and child in Canada. If I take my family comprised of six people and multiply that number by $700, it comes out that the gentlemen opposite are contracting a debt on my behalf of some $4,200. Quite frankly, I think that is excessive and I wish they would not do it.
If we looked at it in another way, it would appear the government is contracting debts on behalf of each taxpayer in the region of $1,500 to $2,000, and I think it should stop that, especially when we consider that the interest payable on that $14 billion amounts to some $2 billion a year. Surely this is excessive. I had no difficulty at all in voting this afternoon in favour of the amendment put forward by the hon. member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) who suggested that the borrowing authority should be for only $8 billion. As a matter of fact, some government members themselves stated that in all probability that is all they would really require. The additional $3 billion or $4 billion was just in case they needed it. They could not present a case for why they might need it and they themselves said that $8 billion is something which would be much more reasonable if they could get their act together and stop mismanaging the financial affairs of the nation. Borrowing $15 billion a year surely guarantees that inflation will continue and that interest rates will have to be maintained at the present high level.
I find it hard to understand when the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) on the one hand and the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) on the other rise in their places and talk about the plight of the old age pensioner, for instance. It is the old age pensioner, the person on a fixed income, who is suffering as a result of the government's inflationary programs, and its inflationary policies, and the type of bill we have before us today makes it quite apparent that the government has no real interest in preventing inflation or in allowing those people who have saved up for their old age
April 6, 1981

to look after themselves. What the government is doing to the elderly people of Canada is drive them to government welfare schemes, the taps of which they turn on and off at will.
With the ever-increasing debt loads on this nation, there will be no incentive to cease borrowing and to prevent inflation because, quite frankly, if I were the deputy minister of finance or the Governor of the Bank of Canada, with the knowledge that inflation is of benefit to the debtor and that the government is the biggest debtor in the land, it would be hard for me to advise a policy of rapidly decreasing inflation. I would not be able to do it and perhaps I would have to suggest a policy of bringing down inflation at a fairly slow rate. But I would not say: No, we are tired of inflation, we have to turn it off because of this accumulated debt. In fact, what we have here with this continuing borrowing and continuing deficit financing, is a self-perpetuating inflationary engine.
Having said that, Mr. Speaker, I want to delve into history for a little while. I want to go back to the time before the eighteenth century when governments borrowed mainly for the purpose of financing their wars. That was the usual reason the sovereign of the day would go to Parliament or to whatever body had the legislative or taxing authority in the country. Before that period, borrowing was done mainly through private lenders. The idea was always there, although it was not always carried out in fact, that at some point in time the sovereign should pay that money back. In the period from 1700 to 1750, mainly in the most developed countries of that day, England and France, the concept of a permanent debt was born.
At the time this happened there was the development of national banking institutions, the forerunners of the central banks, most of which, if not all in the world, are now nationalized banks. There was the establishment of a system of national credit. It was found that the establishment of these institutions and the establishment of a system of permanent debt did much to facilitate trade and the savings of citizens in those countries. It is quite possible that the establishment of this financial system was a prerequisite to the coming of the industrial revolution some 25 to 50 years thereafter.
This permanent debt concept is not seriously questioned today. Once in a while there are members of this House who get up and say they would like to eliminate government debt altogether; but 1 do not think those of us who have really considered the matter would propose such a course of action. The question is not whether national debt should exist but what is the desirable level of that debt? What is equally important is how that debt is to be managed.
We see public debt managed in several ways. For instance, foreign borrowings are used not only in the normal course of our borrowing activities but also as a means of controlling the value of our currency. Occasions not too far in the past can be cited to illustrate where this device has been misused by the government of the day. However, it can be agreed that it is a useful mechanism for keeping steady the level of the Canadian dollar vis-a-vis other world currencies.
Borrowing Authority Act, 1981-82
Most of our debt in this country is domestic, as I guess it is in most developed countries. There are three ways in which domestic borrowing can be accomplished. It can be done through the general public by way of Canada Savings Bonds and other such instruments. It can be done by borrowing from the chartered banks. It can be done by borrowing from the central bank, the Bank of Canada. These three methods are usually used; one in conjunction with the other, and each has certain good points and certain dangers associated with it.
The least inflationary method of borrowing is probably that from the general public, which will not unduly increase the money supply, although it can have the effect of taking so much of the savings out of the citizens' pockets that there is not enough left for private investment in worth-while activities, as was pointed out this afternoon by the hon. member for Edmonton East (Mr. Yurko). For instance, sufficient funds are not left in the economy to finance energy projects in this day and age. Undoubtedly, the form of borrowing which will cause the most excessive inflation is borrowing from the Bank of Canada, which is tantamount to the printing of money. I would urge the government to be a little more careful in the future when it comes to the way in which it manages the debt of this country and the sources from which it borrows.
I would like to address the question of what is the desirable level of debt in Canada. As the hon. member for Thunder Bay-Atikokan Pointed out, it has fluctuated over the years. It has generally been very high during and immediately after time of war. It has been high at other times in the history of Canada, a good example of which is the time at which the construction of the Canadian Pacfic Railway took place. At the time of the construction of that great project the debt of the Government of Canada rose considerably in terms of the gross national product.
1 have pointed out before that over the last few years, since the present Prime Minister took office, the national debt in terms of gross national product has been creeping upward. It seems to me that a prudent government might have a target for the national debt, not in terms of the gross national product of the country, but in relation to the income of the government, roughly in the order of $50 billion a year.
In peacetime, and at a time when there are no Canadian Pacific railways being built, it seems to me a total debt of about twice the income of the government would be a reasonable figure to aim at. That would give us a level of debt of about $100 billion in total. I understand that presently our total debt is somewhat in excess of that. What we see here is a situation which today has been reasonably manageable in total terms but which is now sliding out of control, that is, in terms of the debt we have built up over a period of years.
What should be the additional debt in any one year in terms of the income of the government? It seems to me a reasonable figure a prudent government would try to achieve would be no more than 10 per cent of the public income for any one given year, assuming that there were no national emergencies to deal with. This indicates that a reasonable figure for today is in the region of $5 billion for total annual borrowing. With that figure in mind, $14 billion is clearly out of line.

But what happened this year, last year and what will happen, presumably, next year and in the years to come with the gentlemen over there forming the government is that what has been manageable in the past will not longer be so. The financial affairs of this nation are swiftly becoming unmanageable through the incompetence of a government which is more concerned with ramming through its constitutional ideas rather than addressing the fundamental financial and economic issues which need to be addressed.

To my way of thinking, the peacetime use of borrowed funds should be limited to those things which will benefit future generations, primarily benefit the people who will eventually have to pay those debts. As an example of what could be described as good borrowing, I pointed out the funds borrowed by the Government of Canada to assist in the building of the Canadian Pacific Railway. Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have an opportunity to take part in this debate on Bill C-59. Fiscal matters have always intrigued me. Back in my earlier days when I was involved in municipal politics, I certainly enjoyed the piecing together of the annual budget. I realize that we in this House are dealing with much greater sums of money, but the decisions are still basically the same; who gets what, how much do they get and who pays for it?
What the federal government is asking for is $14 billion, $11 billion of which is provided for in the budget and in the
April 6, 1981

estimates as expenditures and financial requirements to cover that expenditure. The other $3 billion will be set aside for contingency purposes. Since, as the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) has already explained, it is not always possible to predict whether or not Parliament will be sitting at the time this money may be needed, this provision will allow the federal government some flexibility in the future. It is very possible that this $3 billion will not be spent. 1 certainly hope it is not. But if, for example, there is another drought in western Canada like the one experienced last year, or some other such national emergency, we will have the funds available to provide the necessary emergency assistance.
As with any legislation that deals with government financing, the opposition parties want to know what the money will be used for. That is their right, as it is the right of every Canadian to know where their tax dollars are being spent. It will allow all the people in Canada to understand that the federal government turns over a large part of its revenues to the provincial governments. Of the total federal budget for
1981-82, roughly 20 per cent will be turned over to the provincial governments in transfer payments. Established program financing, which includes medicare as well as other cash payments such as equalization payments, and the Canada Assistance Program, are but a few of the many programs under which the federal government transfers expenditures in payments to the provinces. This is, in my view, quite a sizeable sum, and I do not see it getting any smaller in the coming years.
Many times I have heard various people across this country calling on the federal government to curb its spending habits. I would like to take this opportunity to set the record straight, Mr. Speaker, in terms of federal spending.
Over the past five years, total federal expenditures have increased at an average annual rate of 13 per cent, compared with 15 per cent for the provinces as a whole. Serious efforts by the federal government to limit spending on goods and services have borne fruit over the last few years. However, the cost of the public debt has risen sharply and the transfers to the provinces have continued to increase dramatically. Generally speaking, the sudden increase in the federal deficit cannot be attributed to a surge in spending. Spending has increased at a more or less normal rate. What has happened is that federal sources of income and revenue have dropped substantially over the past five years. This type of spending is extremely difficult to reduce, especially in the case of transfers, since they are indexed to inflation.
How do we in the federal government rectify this deteriorating situation? At present, we are locked into a number of federal-provincial cost-sharing programs which are draining our coffers. We have been repeatedly warned by the provinces that we cannot increase our take of revenues from the petroleum industry, even though the multinationals recorded an average after tax profit increase of 54 per cent in 1979.
Borrowing Authority Act, 1981-82
Newfoundland has continuously argued that offshore mineral rights in the Hibernia belong to them, not to the federal government. There is no question that the federal government's revenue sources are decreasing more rapidly than the provinces' but no one has any clues as to where we can go to obtain more revenues.
I believe the time has come to take a good long look at what our priorities are. If we want to bring down the deficit, then let us see what we are spending our money on. As I stated earlier, $13.4 billion is going to be paid to the provinces this year. Now we are told we cannot look for any revenues in their areas of jurisdiction. But if we do not maintain our provincial transfer payments, which are always going to rise because they are indexed to inflation, again we get slammed by the provinces. How do we ever get ahead?
After doing a bit of background research into this matter, I learned that two out of every three federal dollars go toward non-federal programs of one type or another. Many Canadians are not aware of this. Many federal-provincial cost-sharing programs are up for renewal next year under the established programs financing cash payment system. I suggest we look at them very closely to see if some money could be saved there.
I want to see that deficit reduced just as much as any other member of this House. If the provinces want us to continue to spend 20 per cent of our revenues in transfer payments, then they had better get together with us and help to come up with a more rational formula of cost-sharing. It is time to separate our wants from our needs.
In our attempts to keep up with our payments to the provinces and to other levels of government, other important areas of federal concern have had to take a back seat. Twenty-five years ago, the federal government received the equivalent of 17.6 per cent of Canada's total gross national product in revenues, compared to 4.8 per cent for the provinces. As of 1979, the federal share had slipped to 16 per cent, with the provinces jumping up to 25 per cent. I ask, Mr. Speaker, where has that money gone?
When talking about fiscal responsibility, let us call a spade a spade. The federal government has seen its revenue sources increase marginally, while its expenditures continue to grow, especially in terms of its payments to the provinces. On the other hand, the provinces have increased their percentage of the GNP by about 300 per cent while allowing services in many areas to decline. That is partly why there is a federal deficit. That is where we should look for answers to our economic problems.
If the provinces want more power and recognition, then they must be prepared to shoulder more fiscal responsibilities. They cannot have it both ways. This is evident in the housing sector, for example. The federal government builds senior citizens' homes in co-operation with the provincial governments. The federal government funds 90 per cent of the construction costs, with the provincial government paying the other 10 per cent. When it comes time for the official opening of the facility,

Mr. Speaker, I was discussing the subject of Bill C-59, and trying to relate to $14 billion, with my son this morning before I left Peterborough to come to the House of Commons. He asked me exactly how much $14 billion is. My son is 14 years old. I do not suppose there
are very many people in this House who have had the opportunity either in their personal lives or in their businesses to relate to $14 billion in today's terms. I want to relate a couple of things which came to mind this morning.
My son and I tried to discuss the seriousness of the necessity by the government to borrow $14 billion today. I wonder how many people in this House realize that during World War I and World War II, we borrowed less to finance those wars than we are borrowing annually now to finance the deficit spending of this government. This government continues to spend 25 per cent more each year than it takes in.
In order to get an idea of what $14 billion is, perhaps hon. members could picture $10 bills. If we put $10 bills end to end, do hon. members know how far those ten-dollar bills, which we all use in every day trading, would extend? It is 24,000 miles around the world. If you were to put $10 bills end to end, they would travel around the world five and one half times. This government is proposing to borrow 132,000 miles of $10 bills in order to finance its deficit budgeting.
I would like to refer back to the last federal election. In the release that came from the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Bussieres) substantiating the need for Bill C-59 and the borrowing of this excessive amount of money, it reads:
As honourable members will recall, the budget of last October clearly set out this government's strategy of reducing the deficit through restraint in the rate of growth of expenditures.
During the election one short year ago, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) told Canadians what they could expect if they returned him to power. He made five basic commitments during that campaign which he said made up the Libera! party's economic strategy.
This is a good time to look back at that five-point program to see how it relates to today and the need to borrow $14 billion in order to finance this government's spending. When you are running for office it is easy to say you are going to turn things around as soon as you get into power. However, the reality is that things do not change rapidly in government and the economy and the promises of yesterday become the embarrassments of today. The Prime Minister said a year ago, and I quote his words:
The Conservatives have failed miserably in managing the economy, in creating jobs, in controlling inflation, and heading us toward energy security.
These failures would be reversed, he said, by the five-point plan.
The first item in that plan of the last federal election was that the Liberals would "manage more rigorously the nation's finances in order to make more effective use of the taxpayers' money". The Prime Minister made that pledge and he made it very specific. He said "We will hold the line on government expenditure growth under the rate of GNP".
That was the promise in 1979. What is the performance today? The finance minister's budget for the coming fiscal year calls for an increase of 12.8 per cent in total federal
April 6, 1981

spending. It forecasts an increase of 11.1 per cent in the gross national product, including inflation. Therefore, government spending is definitely not being held in line with the GNP.
I wish to quote from an article which appeared in the Ottawa Citizen, written by Charles Lynch:
It's unparliamentary to call people liars, so let's just say that when it comes to talking about spending, it's a wonder the skies don't open to admit a bolt of lightning that would strike the Liberals dead-
Thus we have those wonderful people who brought us the record-breaking deficits and interest payments that have the country reeling, telling us in Johnston's words that "our objective has been, and continues to be, to ensure that taxpayers' dollars spent by the federal government are well spent, and that taxpayers do indeed receive value for money."
I would like to refer to the present government's record of spending in years gone by. Mirabel airport had a cost overrun of $201.7 million; Place du Portage a cost overrun of $92.7 million; the CN Tower in Toronto, $40.5 million; the Pickering airport, $69.3 million; the C.D. Howe building in Ottawa, $45 million; the Paris chancery, $4.4 million; and the discovery train $14.5 million.
In 1976 the Auditor General charged that the government had lost effective control of the public purse. The Lambert royal commission report was released on April 3, 1979. The Liberals responded by announcing a task force to study the report of the task force that had studied the Auditor General's report. The Lambert report observed that:
-the serious malaise pervading the management of government stems fundamentally from a grave weakening, and in some cases an almost total breakdown, in the chain of accountability, first within government, and second in the accountability of government in Parliament and ultimately to the Canadian people.
In conclusion, I will try to complete my 20-minute speech in ten minutes. Overruns in certain departments are very serious problems. The worst department is environment where 153 out of 223 projects were experiencing cost overruns, to a total cost of $283 million. Overruns in the department are equal to 35 per cent of original budgets with 66 per cent experiencing cost overruns. Indian and northern affairs experienced cost overruns on 42 of 76 projects, or 55 per cent of their endeavours.
No government, no family, no business can continue to spend 25 per cent more than it takes in year after year. The taxpayers of Canada are the ones who will lose, the people who put this government in office. I maintain that as soon as we hold government accountable for the money it spends in relation to the money it takes in, the sooner our economy will become sound.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we heard rather a lot of dramatic statements this evening and on Friday about the borrowing authority bill. It may be useful to reiterate, as a number of members on this side of the House have done, that the money for which authority is sought to borrow is all money that will be well accounted for. The budget passed by this House last fall was for approximately $11 billion. Borrowing authority is being sought for that amount plus approximately $3 billion in contingency funds which will be non-lapsing.
Borrowing Authority Act, 1981-82
One member of the official opposition said earlier that the introduction of the non-lapsing amount was new. However, this has been done often in this House before. It was the existence of those non-lapsing funds which allowed the Conservative government to carry on the business of the country during a period last year when Parliament did not meet. Therefore, it is not a new invention but an established way of proceeding.
The moneys expended by the Government of Canada are based on the estimates which are passed by this House. After the event, there is the Auditor General's report which is increasingly becoming an in-depth report. The public accounts committee of this House examines expenditures after the event to ensure that they conform with what was proposed and approved by Parliament in the estimates.
Increasingly the largest portion of moneys spent by the Government are in fact spent in transfers to the provinces or to people. At least 68 per cent of the expenditures of the Government of Canada are transfer payments to the provinces, to the territories, to the municipalities and to people.
Transfer support programs take several forms including grants to support provincial legislatures, hospitals, hospital insurance, medicare and post-secondary education. Transfers to individuals include old age pensions, family allowances, payments under the Canada Pension disability fund and so on.
An earlier criticism was made that the three levels of government borrowing and going into capital markets so extensively was reducing the amounts of money available to the private sector. But I wonder why members of the opposition concentrate only on expenditures of the federal government, when in fact expenditures of provincial and municipal governments have grown at a tremendous rate in recent years, at a rate in excess of the expenditures of the Government of Canada.
About 68 per cent of the total expenditures of the Government of Canada are transfer payments to the provinces or to individuals. The payments which can be controlled directly by the Government of Canada are by far the smallest of the budget. We care very much about having an orderly approach to bond markets but, perhaps even more, we care about transfer payments which are a big part of our social policies directed at assuring that the young who cannot take care of themselves are protected; that children can be educated; that children have access to good medical care; that the old who have small pensions are protected; that by education and programs such as rehabilitation for the disabled and manpower training, we increase the opportunity for Canadians; that Canadians as far as possible have equality of opportunity. These are important programs.
It is important to remember, in the course of complaining about government expenditure, that the government is not spending money for the most part on anything except services to people. Equally, our social policy has been part of the policy on which we were elected. Probably the most important social

April 6, 1981
Borrowing Authority Act, 1981-82
program which exists is related to unemployment and to job creation. Most healthy people, given reasonable jobs, can provide for their own social security to a large extent. For this reason, managing the economy efficiently and fairly is a very big part of the Liberal program, as is our commitment to help those who are unable to help themselves-the young, the old, the sick.
Furthermore, we have heard a lot of talk in the last few days about government intrusion into the private sector. Nobody wants to see the government intruding into the private sector unnecessarily. The private sector should be allowed the freedom to do well what it can do well. But we must face the fact that the record of the private sector in matters such as occupational health and safety and care for the environment has not always been such as to inspire confidence. There is a point where the government must intervene in order to provide fairness, decency and a reasonable quality of life for citizens. It is in this sense that expenditures by government must always be looked at as expenditures on the individual, expenditures concerning which those individuals have a voice and a vote.

Mr. Speaker, I had intended to draw a parallel between Liberal spending leading up to the federal election of May, 1979, when the main issues during that campaign were a matter of fiscal irresponsibility on the part of the government of the day, wrestling inflation to the ground, a commission finding truth in the statements that spending was out of control and that there was a lack of accountability, and the introduction of Bill C-59. Within a year of the election of the government in February, 1980, the deficit jumped from $12 billion to $14 billion. Now the government talks of tackling inflation. It is completely obsessed with a program of legislation which has no relativity to the persons on the street looking for jobs, seeking homes and social legislation, and finding some outlet to which they can relate.
In my remaining time I would like to deal with two simple matters which affect southern Ontario. A number of times I have spoken in the House about the budget introduced in October, 1980, and the regressive discriminatory tax application of excise tax on grape growers and the wine industry. I have indicated that the excise tax, related to the consumer price index, is not in the interests of the Canadian wine industry, the primary grape producers on the Canadian economy. Such automatic quarterly adjustments indicate the defeatist attitude of the government. It also indicates that the government is completely helpless to do anything about the situation. Now taxes are growing and the rate of inflation is out of control.
The consumer price index for the 12-month period ending September 30, 1980, was the base figure for the calculations on which indexing would take place. Thus, we have watched the CPI climb to record levels, as well as the excise tax. Already primary grape growers and wine producers are called upon to make contributions to the revenue departments of both the province and the federal government, far in excess of the normal relationship to their take home pay and the profit margin of the wine industry.
Out of some sympathy and concern for the industry, the government reviewed this tax imposition and made some changes. In the interests of continuing a viable wine and brandy-producing industry, the government should review its program once more as part of its Canadianization program.
Another area of the Canadian economy, that is the marine industry, is being prejudiced by the rigidness of the government's energy policy. As was stated by the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen), the real reason for the imposition of a marine and aviation charge was that foreign fleets and foreign aircraft were purchasing our fuel products. As a result, they were being subsidized by Canadians. Instead of making a practical assessment of its energy policy, the government chose to penalize Canadian flagships engaged in international trade. This government and Canadians should be proud of the record established by the Canadian Great Lakes merchant fleet. Through the efficiency and productivity of its operations that fleet has captured over 93 per cent of the across the border movement.
It is not difficult to understand the importance to our national economy of bulk cargo shipments between Canada and the United States in the heavily undustrialized regions bordering on the Great Lakes. In 1980 the Canadian merchant fleet carried 95 million tonnes of cargo of which over 50 per cent was made up of U.S.-Canada trade generating over $300 million of revenue to this country.
This Canadian industry which provides jobs for Canadians and revenue for Canada should receive treatment equal to that accorded other Canadian industries involved in manufacturing, supplying and the exporting of goods from Canada. To impose the export charges as proposed by forcing Canadian flag ships to pay world prices for fuel oil used in deliveries of iron ore from Labrador to Lake Michigan ports and to pay world prices for fuel oil or coal brought from the United States to Ontario Hydro or the steel mills of Hamilton goes much further than preventing foreign vessels from purchasing bunker fuel at Canadian domestic prices. It imposes a burden on Canadians generally. The proposal as made will add a further $30 million to the operating costs of the Canadian merchant fleet, costs which must be passed on to the consumer. We are those consumers; we will be paying that excess cost. In many instances the imposition of this export charge will likely result in the transfer of shipments to other routes and a diversion of routes which would be less direct and less efficient.
Any federal policy should support and encourage the competitiveness of Canadian industry and promote the exports of this country, but this export charge has just the opposite effect. It will mean a disruption of efficient fleet fuelling and trading patterns. It is difficult to rationalize why the government should provide yet another advantage to railroads and the trucking industry, forms of transport not subject to this fuel cost penalty and less fuel efficient than the Canadian merchant fleet.

If it is neither practical nor possible to introduce a two-price fuel policy. If the government has any concern for the marine industry, then it should introduce a rebate system similar to that which is already in effect in other parts of our economy so that Canadian flag carriers will be in a position to maintain the levels of service and the degree of competitiveness they have attained on the Great Lakes and the St. Lawrence waterway.
I suggest consideration be given to further delay in the implementation of this export charge so that consideration can be given to a review of the allocation of the moneys.
